Comments of the Committee
The Committee has been made sure that the Ministry on its part has been strongly
urging the State Governments/UTs from time to time to come forward expeditiously with

49
feasible proposals. The scheme has gained momentum and so far, 29 States/UTs have set up
State Child Protection Societies, 24 have set up District Child Protection Units and State
Adoption Resource Agencies. Only 5 States have completed the recruitment of staff while
the other States are in the process of doing so. There has been a considerable increase in
the number of CWCs (548), JJB (561), Open shelters (121), Adoption Agencies (196) and
Childline locations (212). Financial support has also been provided for upgradation of 323
and construction of 39 homes for children. The Committee appreciates the efforts of the
Ministry for working as a facilitator for smooth functioning of the scheme. However, the
Committee feels that despite the efforts of the Ministry, a lot remains to be done. Even
though the States have set up the necessary institutional arrangement like the State Child
Protection Societies etc, they are non-functional due to the pending recruitment of staff to
manage these centres. Shortage of required manpower is a major stumbling block in the
implemention of the ICPS Scheme aiming at protection and care of vulnerable children. The
Committee feels that even though the necessary structures have been constructed for
helping distressed children but, they do not serve the desired purpose due to lack of
manpower and other connected facilities. The Committee feels that this scheme is of
significant importance in protecting, helping and taking care of children in vulnerable
situations and the half-hearted efforts for implementation of the scheme would not fulfill
the objectives envisaged for the scheme. The Committee recommends to the Ministry to
give utmost priority to the scheme so as to protect each child in dire situations.
Recommendations/Observations
5.8 The Committee feels that there is a need for stricter control and monitoring of the
institutions of child care so that such cases of harassment and exploitation of children do not take
place, especially by caretakers themselves. The Committee knows that this would only be possible
if these institutions are covered under the Juvenile Justice Act. The Committee recommends to the
Ministry to take up this matter with State Governments on a priority basis as the interest of young
and innocent is at stake. Further, there should be certain criteria laid down for the selection of
caretakers and staff of these institutions. Further, the staff and other workers should be trained
to deal with and take good care of children. The Committee believes that a legislation in this regard
would be a welcome step for the running of such institutions for the welfare of children with strict
monitoring and control.
Action Taken
The Juvenile Justice Act already provides for mandatory registration of all Child Care
Institutions (CCIs) housing children in need of care and protection with the intent of enforcing
minimum standards of care prescribed. Further, the Rules provide for setting up of Children’s
Committees in every institution which are, inter-alia , also encouraged to report incidents of abuse
and exploitation, if any, as well as Management Committees for every Home.
The Ministry has been strongly urging State Governments/UT Administrations from time to
time to identify and register all CCIs under the JJ Act and set up functional Inspection Committees,
Management Committees and Children’s Committees where not available. Copies of the latest
communications sent in this regard are at Annex C.
The Rules under the JJ Act also provide for appropriate training and sensitization of the
staff of the Homes. The Ministry is providing funds to State Governments and UT Administrations
under ICPS for training and sensitization as well, to facilitate good care of children.
To deal with the cases of child sexual abuse in a more effective manner, Ministry of
Women and Child Development has brought in a special law “The Protection of Children from

50
Sexual Offences Act, 2012”. The Act has come into force with effect from 14th November, 2012
along with the rules framed thereunder.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee notes that the Juvenile Justice Act provides for mandatory
registration of all Child Care Institutions functioning in different parts of the country.
However, all such institutions are not registered under the JJ Act. It seems that inspite of
the Ministry pursuing this issue with the State Governments, situation at the ground level
remains unchanged. The Committee is constrained to observe that while duly registered
CCIs need considerable improvement and monitoring, one can only wonder the conditions
prevailing in CCIs operating without any authorization. It is high time that concerted
efforts are initiated both at the Central and State level so as to ensure that children, the
most vulnerable section of our society do not continue to be victimized in the so-called
protection homes.
Recommendations/Observations
5.9 The Committee would also take the opportunity to express its concern about the status of
Child Welfare Committees and Juvenile Justice Boards spread across the country. Feedback given
by the Secretary during her presentation before the Committee confirms its apprehensions about
these bodies which work as watchdogs at the ground level. Lack of functionaries and those in
position not sensitized to the special needs of vulnerable children clearly indicates that much needs
to be done for effective implementation of the restructured ICPS scheme. The Committee feels that
with State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights being in place in most of the States, an
effective monitoring mechanism is already in place. These State Commissions with active co-
ordination with local authorities can easily convert the CWCs and JJBs into vibrant institutions,
keeping a track of child welfare in their area.
Action Taken
Under ICPS, funds are released to the States/UTs, inter-alia, for setting up and management
of JJBs and CWCs with appropriate number of functionaries as prescribed under the JJ Act.
Besides, National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development (NIPCCD) has prepared
training modules for functionaries of these institutions and States/ UTs are being urged by this
Ministry to get the members trained/sensitized. Consequently, 538 CWC Members and 333 JJB
Members have been trained in the year 2011-12 and a number of training programmes are
envisaged in 2012-13 as well. Copies of the latest communications sent by the Ministry in this
regard are at Annex D .
As regards the setting up of SCPCR, 13 States/UTs i.e. Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Delhi,
Goa, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Orissa, Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim and Uttarakhand
have already set up the same and they are gradually being associated in achieving the targets.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee takes a serious view of the not so proper implementation of the
restructured ICPS Scheme. Shortage of functionaries and lack of sensitized and trained
functionaries is a major hurdle in the successful implementation of the scheme. With only
13 States having State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights, the situation seems grim
regarding the efforts made for welfare of children. The Committee would like to reiterate
its earlier recommendation that an effective monitoring mechanism needs to be in place for
proper implementation of the scheme.

Action Taken
As per its mandate RMK provides micro-credit loans to poor women through intermediary
micro-financing organizations (IMOs) like NGOs, VOs etc .
The Loan Agreements are signed between RMK and the intermediary microfinance
organizations (IMOs) before release of loans. The IMOs also submit postdated cheques (PDC)
against the loan dues (principal plus interest). The IMOs are legally bound to perform the loan
obligations as per the Loan Agreement(s). The procedure for Monitoring and Recovery followed in
RMK is enumerated below.
Monitoring of Loans:
(i) The IMOs furnish the utilisation certificates (UCs) in respect of the loan amount
released to them giving entire details viz. name and address of the individual women
beneficiaries, loan amount and purpose and also affix duly attested photos of the women
beneficiaries.

58
After receiving the UC, a post-sanction visit is conducted by another officer (not associated
with the sanction) to verify the utilization of the first disbursement and need assessment for second
disbursement. The second release of 50% is made only after the Kosh is satisfied with the IMOs
utilization of the first release.
Recovery of Loans:
The RMK loans are recoverable from IMOs over a repayment period of 3 years (including
the grace period of 6 months) in quarterly installments along with interest @ 8% per annum on
reducing balance. RMK follows the following procedure for recovery of loans:
(i) The repayment schedule is defined in advance, envisaging quarterly payment of
principal and interest amount. The requisite PDCs are collected as a risk mitigation
measure.
(ii) Demand letters are issued before due dates to all IMOs at pre-defined due dates.
(iii) Quarterly list of defaults is reviewed regularly. Each defaulting NGO is contacted,
either telephonically or through letters, to enquire about the reasons for default and
the likely time for clearing of default.
(iv) The default loans accounts are handled as under:
(a) In the first instance notices are sent to the defaulting IMOs asking them to pay
the overdue amount, urgently.
(b) The defaulting IMO is then sent first reminder, followed by another reminder
and if required final warning (after 30 days from second reminder) to clear the
overdues. If overdues still persist blacklisting is resorted to in case of an NGO
commits default of 4 quarters of interest and/or 4 quarters of principal, or
both. This has been an effective measure of recovery. Blacklisting of the
defaulting IMOs is undertaken mainly to pressurize for urgent clearance of
overdue amounts. In case the IMO clears the loan overdue, it is removed from
RMK black list.
(c) Post-dated cheques given by NGOs are deposited in the concerned banks; if
returned unpaid, case(s) under section 138 of Negotiable Instrument Act (NIA)
are filed in courts.
(d) In case of chronic default, a ‘recall-notice’ is also issued calling the defaulting
IMO to pay upfront the entire outstanding amount of the loan dues, in a
month’s time. If the recall-notice is not complied with, a PDC is lodged for the
entire outstanding dues (loan instalments plus interest).
(e) Suits are filed or wherever applicable, Arbitration Process is followed, to
recover the dues from the NGO where the loan repayment period has been
completed, as per the loan agreement.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is happy to know about the elaborate procedure for monitoring and
recovery of loans is followed in Rashtriya Mahila Kosh (RMK) which provides micro credit
to poor women through intermediary micro-financing organisations (IMOs). The laid out
procedure seems to be satisfactory but its actual efficacy in the monitoring of the IMOs
regarding utilization of the funds is not known. The Committee would like to be apprised

59
about the feedback received by the State authorities regarding the monitoring and recovery
procedure, practical problems, if any, and solutions therefor. The Committee would also like
to know whether the Ministry has started online monitoring of projects sanctioned so as to
identify the erring NGOs easily as the Ministry has not furnished any reply in this respect.
ONE STOP CRISIS CENTRE
Recommendations/Observations
13.1 The Committee observes that a pilot scheme which would serve as an integrated facility
where various needs of victims of violence, such as medical aid, legal assistance, assistance in
filing a police case, counseling and emotional support, temporary shelter for herself and for her
children can be met at a single place, is proposed to be launched in 2012-13. Victims of rape and
sexual assault will also be covered under this scheme.
13.2 The Committee finds that there are already two existing schemes, i.e. Short Stay Homes
and Swadhar which are having, broadly speaking the same objectives and facilities meant for
women/girl victims of social ostracism, crime, violence, victims of trafficking, natural calamities.
Both these schemes provide temporary accommodation, maintenance and rehabilitative services,
counseling, medical facilities. Now, both the schemes are proposed to be merged and renamed as
Swadhar Greh.
13.3 The Committee feels that merger of these two schemes is a wise step. But the Committee
is quite concerned to note that while on the one hand two already existing schemes are proposed
to be merged for more visible impact, the Ministry proposes to launch another new scheme. The
Committee is of the view that Swadhar Grehs equipped with all envisaged facilities can very well
serve as a One Stop Crisis Centre. It is all the more intriguing as already an exercise to consolidate
two similar schemes is on, another new scheme with similar objectives but with a new fancy name
is in the offing. The Committee would like to point out that any new component of the news
scheme, One Stop Crisis Center can be easily made part of the scheme of ‘Swadhar Greh’ .
Action Taken
With regard to Para 13.1 to 13.3, it is stated that Swadhar Scheme was launched by the
Ministry during the year 2001-02 for the benefit of women in difficult circumstances with the
following objectives:
• To provide primary need of shelter, food, clothing and care to the marginalized women/
girls living in difficult circumstances who are without any social and economic support;
• To provide emotional support and counseling to rehabilitate them socially and
economically through education, awareness, etc;
• To arrange for specific clinical, legal and other support for women/girls in need; and
• To provide for helpline or other facilities to such women in distress.
Short Stay Home scheme is being implemented with the objective to rehabilitate women and
girls who are facing social, economic and emotional setback due to family problems, social
ostracism, exploitation, violence or other causes or being forced into prostitution and are in moral
danger.
As the target group and the objectives of Swadhar and Short Stay Home schemes were
similar, these have been merged into a new scheme called ‘Swadhar Greh’ with revised
financial norms in order to reach out to those women who are victims of difficult

60
circumstances and are in need of institutional support for rehabilitation so that they could lead
their life with dignity.
In order to deal with a situation of violence, women require support at various levels that
address their multiple needs. Recognizing this “One Stop Crisis Centre” for women is envisaged
which would serve as an integrated facility where various needs of victims of violence, such as
medical aid, legal assistance, assistance in filing a police case, counseling and emotional support,
temporary shelter for herself and her children and basic necessities for the period of stay can be
met, at a single place. There is a strong need to encourage setting up of One Stop Crisis centre
where women in distress can find immediate legal, medical and counseling services as well as a
help desk of the police under one roof and from where women can be immediately sent to a
shelter.
Victims of rape and sexual assault will also be able to benefit from these Centres where
they will be provided with immediate medical help to deal with her injuries and trauma and where
her statement can be recorded in a conducive and sensitive environment. Such a facility is not
available in Swadhar Greh which is meant to serve as shelter home only with skill development
facility. As such Ministry feels that there is no duplication between the proposed ‘One Stop Crisis
Centre’ and Swadhar and Short Stay Home or its latest manifestation, Swadhar Greh.
Comments of the Committee
Given the increase in the cases of rape, molestation, violence against women in
recent times, the Committee believes that One Stop Crisis Centre which has the objective
to serve as an integrated facility where various needs of victims of violence such as medical
aid, legal assistance etc. at one place assumes great importance. Since the scheme has been
launched in 2012-13, the Committee is of the view that an efficient, well-equipped and
sensitive crisis centre needs to be developed for reaching out to victims of various crimes
and helping them cope up in dire situations. A comfortable and women-friendly environment
would definitely help these victims to deal with their trauma and choose the right course
of action to seek justice for themselves. Care should also be taken to ensure that these
centres themselves should not become homes of despair due to lack of monitoring of their
functioning through inspection.
CENTRAL ADOPTION RESOURCE AUTHORITY (CARA)
Recommendations/Observations
15.5 The Committee would like to highlight that the unauthorized adoption agencies functioning
in the country need to be controlled. Children of some of these institutions often become victims
of trafficking, illegal adoptions and even child labour. The Committee believes that stern measures
need to be taken by the Ministry and CARA against such unauthorized institutions functioning at
present. Either they should mandatorily register themselves with the State Government or face penal
action. This would certainly help in curbing the instances of harassment and exploitation of children
staying in these institutions.
Action Taken
As mentioned in response to para 5.8, the Ministry has been strongly urging State
Governments/UT Administrations from time to time to identify and register all CCIs under the JJ
Act and set up functional Inspection Committees and Management Committees for all homes
including Adoption Agencies. As provided in the JJ Act, all children are to be declared legally free

61
for adoption after a rigorous process by Child Welfare Committees. Thus, trafficking and illegal
adoptions would be curbed when all adoption agencies are registered under the JJ Act.
Further, the registered adoption agencies are also required to regularly update data on
available children and prospective parents on CARA’s adoption portal CARINGS. This also enables
a close watch on the well-being of children in the adoption agencies.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee notes that about 250 adoption agencies are registered in the country.
It is clear that unregistered adoption must also be operating in the country. The Committee
feels concerned about non-compliance of mandatory provision of registration and inspection
of adoption agencies under the JJ Act. The Committee is of the firm view that a nation-
wide survey needs to be taken on an urgent basis so that all adoption agencies are duly
registered and operate in accordance with the prescribed guidelines.
NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN
Recommendations/Observations
16.3 The Committee observes that cases of domestic violence followed by police apathy top the
category of complaints received by NCW. Complaints related to Domestic Violence are forwarded
to concerned authorities under the provisions of the Protection of Women against Domestic
Violence Act, 2005. Inspite of the implementation of the said Act, the situation seems to be grim
for women who face domestic violence. The Committee has been emphasizing upon the proper
implementation of the Act with respect to the proper structure to be put in place along with the
required manpower. The Committee notes that during the Twelfth Plan period, a new scheme is
proposed to be launched whereunder State Governments will be provided assistance for
appointment of Protection Officers and infrastructural support. The Committee feels that with such
an initiative, victims of domestic violence will be getting the required relief.
Action Taken
A Scheme on Assistance to State Governments for implementation of ‘Prevention of Women
from Domestic Violence Act, 2005’ is under finalization in the Ministry. It is hoped that with the
implementation of the scheme the victims of domestic violence are likely to get the required relief.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is constrained to observe that a Scheme on Assistance to State
Governments for implementation of ‘Prevention of Women from Domestic Violence Act,
2005’ which was proposed to be launched during the Twelfth Plan period is yet to be
finalized. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act was enacted in 2005, i.e.
during the Eleventh Plan period. However, its implementation is yet to take off in the real
sense. The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry to expedite the finalization
of the proposed scheme, and set all formalities duly completed so that victims can be
benefitted as envisaged under the Act.
Recommendations/Observations
16.4 Apart from this, the Committee believes that a vigorous awareness generation programme
through various mediums, especially television should be undertaken by NCW with special focus
on offices, colleges/universities, schools etc. Women need to know their rights and the platform

62
for redressal of their grievances. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a pro-active role
should be played by NCW not just for redressal of complaints but also their prevention. Secondly,
short-training and awareness generation programme should be organized by NCW for the police
personnel in various States/UTs so as to sensitize and educate the police personnel about the
assistance to be given to women who are victims of various crimes etc.
Action Taken
The National Commission for Women has come up with various awareness generation
programmes like Mahila Adhikar Abhiyan to reach the grassroots level and create awareness among
women on women’s rights.
Such campaigns could reach effectively the women particularly those in rural and remote
areas of the country and create and impact the minds of people about women’s issues.
The Commission has produced audio – video spots highlighting the issues of Domestic
Violence, Dowry, NRIs, PC&PNDT Act and had awareness campaigns through Radio C&S
channels and Doordarshan to have better reach in the society.
The Commission has undertaken a scheme for capacity building of judicial and police
officials to sensitize officials with regard to gender problems.
To sensitize and educate the police and judicial officials about women related laws, the
Commission has organized training programmes with Maharashtra Judicial Academy, Amity Law
School, Noida, Police Training Centre in Mumbai, Haryana Police Academy, Madhuban and
Rajasthan Police Academy, Rajasthan.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is of the firm belief that the NCW being a national body for women
should play a vibrant and vigorous role in safeguarding the interests of women. Apart from
addressing the grievances of women on their complaints, NCW engages in promotional
research, hold awareness generation programmes, organize workshops/consultation etc.
Taking into cognizance the sad reality of rising crime against women, the Committee feels
that a national body like NCW needs to give voice to all the helpless women for bringing
about the desired change in the legal framework of the country, social and cultural mindset
and position of women in public and private sphere. NCW should undertake surveys and
research projects for highlighting and addressing the harsh and critical plight of women in
distressed circumstances. The Committee hopes that meaningful and serious efforts would
be made by the NCW for educating, changing and sensitizing the society about rights of
women and legal protection given to them and importance of providing a safe and secure
environment for women across the country through various means such as media, street
plays, meetings etc. The need of the hour is to create and spread awareness about issues
of women and promote further gender equality and safety.
CONVERGENCE OF SCHEMES
Recommendations/Observations
18.1 It has been the observation of the Committee that there are several schemes for both
women and child welfare administered by different Ministries or State Governments with similar
objectives. This leads some times to over-lapping of schemes which may not be fruitful for the
targeted beneficiaries. The Committee feels that there is a need for convergence of schemes with

63
more or less same vision and objectives. Co-ordination with different Ministries/Departments at
various levels is required for such convergence of services with various scheme/programmes of the
different implementing Ministries. This convergence of services would help in better delivery of
services and also help in increasing the out-reach of the schemes to more number of beneficiaries.
The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to have an evaluation done of its schemes
which may require convergence and co-ordination with schemes of other Departments/Ministries/
State Governments and make concerted efforts in this regard.
Action Taken
The Hon’ble Committee’s observations are noted for compliance.
Comments of the Committee
The Committee is dismayed to note the reply of the Ministry on its observations/
recommendations on the very crucial issue of convergence of schemes. The Committee
reiterates its observation and once again recommends that the Ministry may take on
priority basis evaluation of schemes which may require convergence and co-ordination with
schemes of other Departments/Ministries/State Governments and take appropriate measures
accordingly. Intention of the Committee behind this observation is to ensure the reach of
well-conceived and properly structured Schemes to the targeted beneficiaries.

OBSERV ATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE — AT A GLANCE
I. BUDGETERY ALLOCATION
The Committee is constrained to observe that though the utilization figure for funds
allocated for the Ministry for the year 2011-12 increased to `15604.44 crore with maximum
utilization indicated in the ICDS scheme, there were many schemes which witnessed a very
low level of utilization or even nil utilization like Rashtriya Mahila Kosh, Swayam Siddha,
Relief and Rehabilitations of Rape Victims, World Bank ICDS IV Project, National Nutrition
Mission, Conditional Cash Transfer Scheme for Girl Child with Insurance Cover, Hostels for
Working Women, National Mission for Empowerment of Women, Priyadarshini, Information,
Mass Education and Publication. With respect to the National Mission for Empowerment of
Women, the Committee has been given to understand that this Centrally Sponsored Scheme
was approved by the Planning Commission in the beginning of April, 2011. Since the budget
for the Mission involved expenditure for setting up of units deploying dedicated manpower
both for the State Resource Centre for Women as well as the pilot projects in the State/
UT, considerable time was being taken by the State Governments for completion of
formalities for the operationalisation of the units. The Committee is of the view that urgent
attention of the Ministry is required to motivate the State Governments to complete all
formalities in a time-bound manner so that implementation of the National Mission for
Empowerment of Women is not further delayed. The Committee also takes a serious view
of under-utilization of funds with respect to other schemes of the Ministry which are being
implemented for the welfare of women and children. The need of the hour is to identify
problem areas, if any, in utilization of funds and also completion of other formalities with
active co-operation and co-ordination of the State Governments and a mission mode
approach is required for effective implementation of all these women/child centric schemes.
(Para 2.5)
The Committee takes a serious view of the under-utilization of allocated funds due
to procedural delays in initiating a scheme, delays in other preparatory exercises, non-
receipt of viable proposals from the State Governments or lack of a system in place for
implementation and monitoring as these factors could have been easily foreseen and avoided
by the Department. The Committee believes that the mandate of the Ministry is of
immense importance as it caters to the needs and welfare of women and children who are
vulnerable sections of our country. The very purpose of any scheme introduced for the
welfare of women and children is defeated if funds are not utilized to an optimum level and
in time leading not only to poor implementation of the scheme but also reductions in
allocations by the Government in coming years. This also means that the benefits of the
scheme will not reach the targeted beneficiaries. Time and again, the Committee has been
reiterating on optimum and judicious utilization of funds for various schemes being
implemented for women and children. The Committee feels that the Ministry needs to focus
upon the timely utilization of funds and proper implementation of the schemes for efficient
delivery of services with a well placed monitoring mechanism to oversee the work done.
(Para 2.6)
The Committee notes that the two schemes of the Ministry i.e. SABLA and IGMSY
were introduced in the year 2010-11 and there were lot of preparatory activities/exercises
to be conducted by the State Governments for their implementation which led to savings
65

66
with respect to funds allocated for them. Savings or unspent balances of `276.42 crore and
`290.37 crore as on 1.4.12 has been reported by the Ministry for SABLA and IGMSY
respectively. The Committee observes that with such a large amount of unspent balances,
it can be said that the proper implementation of the scheme is yet to take off. The noble
objective of the scheme remain only on paper and is not translated into benefiting girls/
women. The Committee has repeatedly reiterated the fact that preparatory exercise needs
to be completed as early as possible so that the implementation of the scheme does not
suffer. The Committee hopes that this financial year would see the completion of all such
exercise and formalities leading to effective implementation of the scheme.
As regards the ICDS Scheme, the Committee has been given to understand that the
ICDS Scheme was not receiving adequate budgetary provision at BE stage, resulting in
additional allocation through supplementary demands for grants and re-appropriation out of
savings from other schemes of the Ministry at the end of the financial year. This also
resulted in release of funds to States/UTs in the last week of March. There was no proper
fund flow mechanism/devolution of financial powers in most of the States/UTs for timely
utilization of funds, causing sub-optional delivery of services and implementation of scheme
including utilization of funds. The Ministry has pointed out that the system of financing the
scheme was partly responsible for unspent money or shortfall with the States causing
imbalances. Communication with the Chief Ministers/Administrators of the States/UTs had
been facilitated by the Ministry for utilization of funds for the ICDS Scheme. Excess
expenditure or unspent balance lying with the State during the last financial year was to
be adjusted at the time of release of funds during the third installment in the third quarter
of the financial year. The Government of India had approved the Ministry’s proposal for
strengthening and restructuring of ICDS on 24.09.2012 with an allocation of `1,23,580 crore
during the 12th Plan Period. The shortcomings in the scheme were likely to be taken care
of through instrument and modalities of financial management.
The Committee is of view that ICDS Scheme is one of the most important schemes
of the Ministry of Women and Child Development benefiting women and children.
Therefore, there should not be any dearth of funds for this scheme. Further, timely release
of funds to the States should be facilitated and utilization certificates should be sought for
the expenditure incurred in proper time. Reiterating on the importance of the scheme, the
Committee believes that serious and concerted efforts need to be made for efficacious and
timely implementation of the scheme. Since the strengthening and restructuring of ICDS
Scheme is being envisaged, the Committee hopes that all the shortcomings of the scheme
would be taken care of as assured by the Ministry. However, a strong sense of dedication
and will is required at the level of the Ministry to make the ICDS Scheme a success.
(Para 2.9)
The Committee notes that the Ministry is taking the issue of unspent balances with
regard to ICDS Scheme, SABLA and IGMSY seriously. The Committee has been given to
understand that the matter of unspent balances was regularly being taken up with the
States/UTs. Apart from monitoring and supervision mechanism, the States/UTs have to
submit physical and financial progress report in each quarter and Annual Progress Report
too. The Committee has been reiterating on proper utilization of funds so that the problem
of unspent balances does not crop up as it should not lead to hasty utilization of funds but
judicious and optimum use of funds has to be ensured as well. The Committee also
appreciates the idea of the Ministry to conduct evaluation of the SABLA and IGMSY
Schemes by an independent agency. (Para 2.10)
The Committee has been apprised that the number of Utilization Certificates
outstanding as on 30th June, 2012 with respect to grants released upto 31st March, 2012

67
was 4987 as against 5129 pending on 31st March, 2012 which works out to be only 42 UCs
being liquidated during the year 2012-13 as compared to liquidation of 548 UCs in the year
2011-12 indicating that, the process of liquidation of UCs in the year 2012-13 has been
extremely slow and disappointing. The Committee would like to emphasize upon the
importance of liquidating the pending UCs for ensuring accountability of funds. The
Committee would like to reiterate its earlier recommendation of making consistent and
concerted efforts to be made by the Ministry for liquidation of pending UCs. The progress
of this liquidation needs to be monitored regularly so that there is no laxity in the process
as evident from the less number of liquidated UCs. (Para 2.11 & 2.12)
III. INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICE (ICDS) SCHEME
The Committee has been given to understand that the draft findings of the NCAER
study on ICDS especially in respect of supply of supplementary nutrition, status of AWC
infrastructure, availability of basic kits etc. were shared with the States for taking
necessary action on their part. Some of the shortcomings pointed out in the study were
again highlighted in the review of ICDS Scheme with State Secretaries held on 13-14
September, 2012. The Ministry had provided detailed comments on the draft report for its
finalization with NCAER in August 2010. The Ministry had not agreed to some of the
findings of the NCAER due to factual incorrectedness. The Committee would like to be
apprised about the points/aspects not agreed to by the Ministry. Further, the Committee
wonders about the follow-up action taken by the States/UTs and the Ministry after sharing
the findings of the NCAER study. The Committee is aware of the fact that the
Government has approved the Ministry’s proposal for strengthening and restructuring of
ICDS to address several gaps, systematic, management and institutional arrangement for
its better implementation. The Committee would like to point out that if no specific
efforts are being made by the Ministry to address the shortcomings in the ICDS Scheme,
especially relating to supplementary nutrition, infrastructure of AWC, availability of basic
kits etc. as highlighted by the NCAER study, there does not seem to be much hope for
the scheme’s success even when it would be restructured and strengthened. The success
of a scheme depends on identification of shortcomings, if any, in its implementation and
addressing them as early as possible by making serious efforts. The Committee,
therefore, hopes that necessary measures would be taken by the Ministry in this regard.
(Para 3.2 & 3.3)
The Committee had expressed its concern regarding non-availability of adequate
funds for the strengthening and restructuring of the ICDS Scheme. With an allocation of
half of `30,000 crore, which the Ministry had requested for, the Committee wonders as to
how the Ministry envisages to start the strengthening and restructuring exercise of the
ICDS Scheme. Against this backdrop, the issue of unspent balances becomes of critical
importance as the requirement of additional funds for this flagship scheme needs to be
justified by optimum and judicious utilization of resources. The Committee feels that mere
delegation of requisite financial powers to the officers in the State/UT Women and Child
Development Departments dealing with ICDS will not help. A proper monitoring mechanism
for supervising utilization of funds and getting statements of expenditure incurred on time
needs to be focussed upon. (Para 3.9, 3.10 & 3.11)

IV. RAJIV GANDHI NATIONAL CRECHE SCHEME FOR WORKING MOTHERS
The Committee has been apprised that the following feedback has been given by the
model creches set up on pilot basis in Delhi with enhanced financial norms:
– provision for rent is not sufficient under the proposed revised scheme.
– Importance of nutrition supplementation with enhanced grant in addressing the
issue of malnutrition.
– Increase in honorarium from `1000 to `3000 has helped in getting better quality
teachers. Wages under the revised scheme should be on par with the Anganwadi
workers.
– Budget for model creches should include provision for contingency for
miscellaneous expenditure such as fuel for cooking, electricity, water etc.

if the coverage of revised creche scheme is expended.
The Committee finds that the feedback received from the implementing agencies as
mentioned above is of immense importance and that the shortcomings in the scheme should
be taken care of in the revised and restructured scheme with enhanced cost norms. The
Committee would like to place special emphasis on training of workers working in the
creches who should be more sensitive to the needs of the children. However, increased
honorarium at par with A WWs would definitely attract  qualified workers/teachers. The
Committee, therefore, recommends to the Ministry to bring about the desired changes in
the scheme by alleviating all the problem areas and implement the revised scheme with
revised norms as soon as possible. (Para 4.4)
V. INTEGRATED CHILD PROTECTION SCHEME (ICPS)
The Committee has been made sure that the Ministry on its part has been strongly
urging the State Governments/UTs from time to time to come forward expeditiously with
feasible proposals. The scheme has gained momentum and so far, 29 States/UTs have set up
State Child Protection Societies, 24 have set up District Child Protection Units and State
Adoption Resource Agencies. Only 5 States have completed the recruitment of staff while the
other States arc in the process of doing so. There has been a considerable increase in the
number of CWCs (548), JJB (561), Open shelters (121), Adoption Agencies (196) and Childline
locations (212). Financial support has also been provided for upgradation of 323 and
construction of 39 homes for children. The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Ministry
for working as a facilitator for smooth functioning of the scheme. However, the Committee
feels that despite the efforts of the Ministry, a lot remains to be done. Even though the States
have set up the necessary institutional arrangement like the State Child Protection Societies
etc, they are non-functional due to the pending recruitment of staff to manage these centres.
Shortage of required manpower is a major stumbling block in the implemention of the ICPS
Scheme aiming at protection and care of vulnerable children. The Committee feels that even
though the necessary structures have been constructed for helping distressed children but,
they do not serve the desired purpose due to lack of manpower and other connected facilities.
The Committee feels that this scheme is of significant importance in protecting, helping and
taking care of children in vulnerable situations and the half-hearted efforts for
implementation of the scheme would not fulfill the objectives envisaged for the scheme. The
Committee recommends to the Ministry to give utmost priority to the scheme so as to protect
each child in dire situations. (Para 5.6)

71
The Committee notes that the Juvenile Justice Act provides for mandatory
registration of all Child Care Institutions functioning in different parts of the country.
However, all such institutions are not registered under the J.J Act. It seems that inspite
of the Ministry pursuing this issue with the State Governments, situation at the ground
level remains unchanged. The Committee is constrained to observe that while duly
registered CCIs need considerable improvement and monitoring, one can only wonder the
conditions prevailing in CCIs operating without any authorization. It is high time that
concerted efforts are initiated both at the Central and State level so as to ensure that
children, the most vulnerable section of our society do not continue to be victimized in the
so-called protection homes. (Para 5.8)
The Committee takes a serious view of the not so proper implementation of the
restructured ICPS Scheme. Shortage of functionaries and lack of sensitized and trained
functionaries is a major hurdle in the successful implementation of the scheme. With only
13 States having State Commissions for Protection of Child Rights, the situation seems grim
regarding the efforts made for welfare of children. The Committee would like to reiterate
its earlier recommendation that an effective monitoring mechanism needs to be in place for
proper implementation of the scheme. (Para 5.9)

evaluate and assess if the structures are not in place. The Committee, accordingly,
recommends to the Ministry to co-ordinate with the States/UTs to utilize the funds properly

Committee fecls that the exercise of convergence with various schedules of the Ministries
needs to be focused upon for strengthening the non-nutrition component of the scheme.

IX. INDIRA GANDHI MATRITV A SAHYOG YOJANA (lGMSY)
The IGMSY Scheme was approved in 2010 and the year 2011-12 was the first
complete year of implementation of the Scheme. The Committee has been given to
understand that there was under-utilization of funds due to the fact that the States/UTs had
to undertake a lot of preparatory exercises such as establishment of cells at States and
district levels, tie up with Banks and post-office etc. along with compliance with procedural
formalities involved in the cash transfer to the beneficiaries. The Committee understands
the fact that many preparatory exercises need to be completed before the proper
implementation of any scheme. However, these preparatory exercises need to be completed
within the first year of the implementation of the scheme itself or else the delay in its
completion would further cause delay in the implementation of the scheme. The Committee
hopes that by now the preparatory exercises and other formalities with respect to IGMSY
Scheme are supposedly complete and the actual implementation of the Scheme has begun
in the year 2012-13 leading to optimum utilization of funds. In case, it is not completed,
it should be taken up on priority basis. (Para 9.3)

in the last two years. The Committee strongly believes that States need to be reminded and
motivated about submission of viable proposals for the implementation of this scheme which
ensures sustainable employment for the poor and asset-less rural and urban women across
the country. The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the Ministry should make all out
efforts for effective utilization of funds, especially in the North Eastern States so that the
benefits of the scheme reach the poor and asset-less women. (Para 10.5 & 10.6)
XI. RASHTRIYA MAHILA KOSH (RMK)
The Committee notes that RMK is one of the most important schemes for
empowering the poor women and provides finance for their projects. This scheme is being
restructured since the. last three years. EFC note has been circulated and one meeting of
the EFC has already taken place. The Committee is, however, not happy with the slow pace
of the restructuring exercise being undertaken. The Committee, therefore, recommends
that the restructuring exercise of RMK should be completed expeditiously so that the
scheme can be implemented without delay and its benefits reach the targeted beneficiaries
in time and that such procedural delays need to be avoided or curtailed, and that the
allocation for the scheme is utilized effectively for the implementation of the revamped
scheme. (Para 11.3)
The Committee notes that action has been initiated by RMK for a countrywide
survey of impact of RMK loans on poor women beneficiaries from 500 women SHGs

73
covering over 1500 women beneficiaries from Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Delhi, MP,
Maharashtra, Orissa, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu and West Bengal. While welcoming this move,
the Committee would like to point out that a sample study covering Andhra Pradesh,
Orissa, Tamil Nadu and Rajasthan has already been conducted in two phases. It would have
been better if some other States, especially from N-E Region and Northern Region had been
included. The Committee strongly feels that only then it could be said that assessment has
been made in the real sense. The Committee, accordingly, recommends that States from
these two regions may be included. (Para 11.6)
The Committee is happy to know about the elaborate procedure for monitoring and
recovery of loans is followed in Rashtriya Mahila Kosh (RMK) which provides micro credit
to poor women through intermediary micro-financing organisations (IMOs). The laid out
procedure seems to be satisfactory but its actual efficacy in the monitoring of the IMOs
regarding utilization of the funds is not known. The Committee would like to be apprised
about the feedback received by the State authorities regarding the monitoring and recovery
procedure, practical  problems, if any, and solutions therefor. The Committee would also like
to know whether the Ministry has started online monitoring of projects sanctioned so as to
identify the erring NGOs easily as the Ministry has not furnished any reply in this respect.
(Para 11.8)
XIII. ONE STOP CRISIS CENTRE
Given the increase in the cases of rape, molestation, violence against women in
recent times, the Committee believes that One Stop Crisis Centre which has the objective
to serve as an integrated facility where various needs of victims of violence such as medical
aid, legal assistance etc at one place assumes great importance. Since the scheme has been
launched in 2012-13, the Committee is of the view that an efficient, well-equipped and
sensitive crisis centre needs to be developed for reaching out to victims of various crimes
and helping them cope up in dire situations. A comfortable and women-friendly environment
would definitely help these victims to deal with their trauma and choose the right course
of action to seek justice for themselves. Care should also be taken to ensure that these
centres themselves should not become homes of despair due to lack of monitoring of their
functioning through inspection. (Para 13.1, 13.2 & 13.3)
XV. CENTRAL ADOPTION RESOURCE AUTHORITY (CARA)
The Committee notes that about 250 adoption agencies are registered in the country.
It is clear that unregistered adoption must also be operating in the country. The Committee
feels concerned about non-compliance of mandatory provision of registration and inspection
of adoption agencies under the JJ Act. The Committee is of the firm view that a nation-
wide survey needs to be taken on an urgent basis so that all adoption agencies are duly
registered and operate in accordance with the prescribed guidelines. (Para 15.5)
XVI. NA TIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN
The Committee is constrained to observe that a Scheme on Assistance to State
Governments for implementation of ‘Prevention of Women from Domestic Violence Act,
2005' which was proposed to be launched during the Twelfth Plan period is yet to be
finalized. The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act was enacted in 2005, i.e.
during the Eleventh Plan period. However, its implementation is yet to take off in the real
sense. The Committee would like to impress upon the Ministry to expedite the finalization
of the proposed scheme, and set all formalities duly completed so that victims can be
benefited as envisaged under the Act. (Para 16.3)

74
The Committee is of the firm belief that the NCW being a national body for women
should play a vibrant and vigorous role in safeguarding the interests of women. Apart from
addressing the grievances of women on their complaints, NCW engages in promotional
research, hold awareness generation programmes, organize workshops/consultation etc.
Taking into cognizance the sad reality of rising crime against women, the Committee feels
that a national body like NCW needs to give voice to all the helpless women for bringing
about the desired change in the legal framework of the country, social and cultural mindset
and position of women in public and private sphere. NCW should undertake surveys and
research projects for highlighting and addressing the harsh and critical plight of women in
distressed circumstances. The Committee hopes that meaningful and serious efforts would
be made by the NCW for educating, changing and sensitizing the society about rights of
women and legal protection given to them and importance of providing a safe and secure
environment for women across the country through various means such as media, street
plays, meetings etc. The need of the hour is to create and spread awareness about issues
of women and promote further gender equality and safety. (Para 16.4) -
XVIII. CONVERGENCE OF SCHEMES
The Committee is dismayed to note the reply of the Ministry on its observations/
recommendations on the very crucial issue of convergence of schemes. The Committee
reiterates its observation and once again recommends that the Ministry may take on
priority basis evaluation of schemes which may require convergence and co-ordination with
schemes of other Departments/Ministries/State Governments and take appropriate measures
accordingly. Intention of the  Committee behind this observation is to ensure the reach of
well-conceived and properly structured Schemes to the targeted beneficiaries. (Para 18.1)

Dear Shri Dwivedi,
This is to share my deep concern regarding the abuse and neglect of children living in
orphanages and other Child Care Institutions (CCIs), reported by the Media in many States across
the country. It has emerged that most of these incidences have occurred in Institutions/Orphanages
which are not registered under the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000
(JJ ACT).
As you may be aware, Section 34(3) of the JJ Act provides for mandatory registration of
all CCIs housing children in need of care and protection with the intent of enforcing minimum
standards of care for the services provided to children in the Homes. The JJ Act also provided
for mechanisms for stringent monitoring of the quality of services. It is for this reason that this
Ministry has been persistently urging the State Governments/UT Administrations to identify and
register all CCIs under the JJ Act. However, the progress in this regard is very slow.
To ensure that children in all the Homes receive the best of care, and are not subject to
abuse and neglect, it is imperative that all the homes running in your State which house children
in need of care and protection, be immediately identified and registered under the JJ Act.
I, therefore, suggest that the State Government may, through public advertisements, invite
the attention of all organizations running facilities for children in need of care and protection
towards their obligation for registration under the JJ Act. Simultaneously, surveys may be
conducted at the district level to identify such homes that are not registered and the organization
may be urged to register under the Act immediately failing which their registration/recognition/
license under any other legislation may be withdrawn and the children shifted to other residential
Homes under the JJ Act.
I understand that some of these Homes/orphanages are licensed under the Women and
Children Institutions (Licensing) Act, 1956 (WCLA), or recognized under the Orphanages and other
Charitable Homes (Supervision and Control) Act 1960 (OCHA), as may be applicable in the State,
it is not known, which of these legislations is applicable in your State, and whether there is a
functional mechanism in place for monitoring institutions under these Acts. I understand that many
children in need of care and protection are also living in other facilities such as homes being run
by religious institutions, homes for differently-abled children etc. I would greatly appreciate if the
status in this regard is reviewed and a report is sent to the Ministry.

89
The Ministry is contemplating further strengthening of Section 34(3) of the JJ Act, inter-
alia to provide strict penalties for non-registration, and considering repeal of clauses related to
child care institutions in the earlier Acts (WCLA and OCHA). May I request your comments and
suggestions in this regard also?
I would be grateful if this exercise is completed within a period of one month and
information sent to the Ministry by 20
th April, 2012.
With regards,
Yours sincerely,

Provisions in JJ Act for Monitoring of Homes
(a) Section 34 (3) of the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2000 (JJ Act)
provides for mandatory registration of all Child Care Institution (CCI) housing children
in need of care and protection with the intent of enforcing minimum standards of care for
the services provided for children in these Homes.
(b) Section 35  of the JJ Act provides appointment of the inspection committees  by the State
Governments for the State, a district and city, as the case may be, for the Children’s Homes.
The Committee is required to have representatives from the State Government, Child Welfare
Committee, voluntary organisations as well as medical experts and social workers.
Rule 60  provides for constitution of inspection committee on recommendation of selection
committee under Rule 91. The Inspection Committee (not less than 3 members together) is
required to visit every institution once in 3 months , either with prior intimation or on
surprise visit. It is to oversee the conditions in the Homes and appropriateness of the
processes for safety, well-being, standards of care for children and also look out for cases
of child rights violation.
Reports are to be submitted to State Governments and DCPU.
So far inspection committees have been constituted by 15 State/UTs, namely, Andaman &
Nicobar Islands, Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar, Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh, Delhi, Goa, Haryana,
Karnataka, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram, Nagaland, Punjab and Sikkim.
(c) Section 36 of the JJ Act provides for Social Audit  under the Act for monitoring and
evaluation of institutions. Rule 66  provides for annual monitoring .and evaluation by Central
or State Government of the implementation of the Act, including, inter alia , functioning of
institutions. Social Audit is to be done with support and involvement of organisations working
in the field of mental health, child care and protection NIPCCD, ICCW, CIF, SSWBs , Schools
of Social Work and Schools of Law.
(d) Chapter VI of the Model Rules framed under the JJ Act provides minimum standards of
care to be maintained in the Homes including physical infrastructure; staff; daily need of the
child including food; clothing; medicines; education; vocational training; management of
individual case file; provision of Inspection Committee and Children Committee etc.
(e) Rule 60  of the Model Rules framed under the JJ Act also prescribes comprehensive measures
to respond in case of any kind of abuse, including sexual abuse, neglect and maltreatment is
noticed in the CCI.
(f) Rule 25 (p) of the Model Rules framed under the JJ Act provides that Child Welfare
Committee shall visit each institution where children are sent for care and protection or
adoption at least once in three months to review the condition of children in institutions,
with support of the State Government and suggest necessary action.
(g) Rule 55 of the provides for setting up of a Management Committee for every institution
for the management of the institution and monitoring the progress of every juvenile and child.
The Management Committee is required to consist of the following personnel:
91

92
District Child Protection Officer (District Child Protection Unit)
Chairperson
(If DCPU not constituted, District Magistrate or Collector or his nominee)
Officer-in-charge - Member
Secretary
Probation Officer or Child Welfare Officer or Case Worker - Member
Medical Officer - Member
Psychologist or Counsellor - Member
Workshop Supervisor or Instructor in V ocation - Member
Teacher - Member
Social Worker Member of Juvenile Justice Board or
Child Welfare Committee - Member
A juvenile or child representative from each of the Children’s
Committees (on a monthly rotation basis to ensure
representation of juveniles or children from all age groups) - Member
Representatives from voluntary organizations - Special invitee
involved in providing professional and
technical services like education, vocational
training, psychosocial care, mental health
intervention and legal aid
The Management Committee shall meet every month to consider and review inter alia  the
facilities in the Home, individual problems of juveniles and children, provision of legal aid
services, vocational training, education and life skills development programmes, review of
progress, adjustment and modification of residential programmes to the needs of the juveniles
and children etc.
(h) Rule 56 of the Model Rules provides for facilitation of setting up of Children’s Committees
in every institution by the Officer-in-Charge for three different age groups of 6-10 years,
11-15 years and 16-18 years. Such Committee is required to meet every month and
encouraged to participate in following activities:
(a) improvement of the condition of the institution;
(b) reviewing the standards of care being followed;
(c) preparing daily routine and diet scale;
(d) developing educational, vocational and recreation plans;
(e) supporting each other in managing crisis;
(f) reporting abuse and exploitation by peers and caregivers;
(g) creative expression of their views through wall papers or newsletters or paintings or
music or theater;
(h) management of institution through the Management Committee.

93
The Officer-in-Charge shall ensure that the Children’s Committees maintain a register for
recording the activities and proceedings, and place it before the Management Committee in
their monthly meetings.
The Management Committee shall seek a report from the Officer-in-Charge on the setting
up and functioning of the Children’s Committees, review these reports in their monthly
meetings and take necessary action where required.
(i) Rule 55 (7) of the Model Rules provides for setting up of a complaint and redress
mechanism in every institution. and a Children’s Suggestion Box is required to be
installed in every institution at a place easily accessible to juveniles and children away from
the office set up and closer to the residence or rooms or dormitories of the children. The key
to the Suggestion’ Box shall remain in the custody of the Chairperson of the Management
Committee and shall be checked every week by the him or his representative from District
Child Protection Unit, in the presence of the members of the Children’s Committees.
If there is a problem or suggestion that requires immediate attention, the Chairperson of the
Management Committee shall call for an emergency meeting of the Management Committee to
discuss and take necessary action. The quorum for conducting the emergency meetings shall
be five members, including two members of Children’s Committees, Chairperson of the
Management Committee, Member of Committee or the Board as the case may be and the
Officer-in-Charge of the institution.
In the event of a serious allegation or complaint against the Officer-in-Charge of the
institution, he shall not be part of the emergency meeting and another available member
of the Management Committee shall be included in his place.
All suggestions received through the suggestion box and action taken as a result of the
decisions made in the emergency meeting or action required to be taken are required to be
placed for discussion and review in the monthly meeting of the Management Committee.
(j) The Rules also provide for a Children’s Suggestion Book to be maintained in every
institution where the complaints and action taken by the Management Committee are duly
recorded and such action and follow up shall be communicated to the Children’s Committees
after every monthly meeting of the Management Committee. The Board or Committee is
required to review the Children’s Suggestion Book at least once in three months.

mechanisms for monitoring the management of the Homes through Inspection Committees and

Secretaries and Principal Secretaries of State Governments in this regard and I request you to
kindly issue instructions so that speedy action is taken to ensure that all Homes are properly

CHAPTER-I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV A TIONS, WHICH
HA VE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
III. SARV A  SIKSHA ABHIYAN/RIGHT TO EDUCATION
Recommendations/observations
3.36 It is evident that by the time students come to class VIII their performance in mathematics,
science and social sciences declines considerably. With the exception of language, where pass
percentage is 60 per cent, the pass percentage of class VIII students in mathematics, science and
social sciences remains around 40 to 45 per cent only. Committee’s attention was also drawn to
the findings of the Annual Status of Education Report (ASER), Seventh Survey, which highlighted
some negative facts about the learning capacity of children. According to this survey, the
proportion of children in standard V able to read a standard II level text book had dropped from
53.07 per cent in 2010 to 48.2 per cent in 2011, particularly in the Northern States. Department’s
clarification on this point was that the curriculum and text books were designed to have unrealistic
expectations of children and that textbooks required urgent revisions. This issue of curriculum
revision/reform has already been taken up with the States and an advisory on quality has also been
issued by the Department. The Committee hopes that the initiatives of the Department would result
in some positive improvements in learning enhancement of the children. One way out could be
evolving the concept of peer education system within the school as a means of learning
enhancement. Under this concept, a higher grade student can adopt a lower grade student and start
teaching him. This would help the teaching student to make his base strong. As an incentive to
the teaching student, a provision of stipend could also be made. This peer education concept could
go a long way in enhancing the learning capacity of the children. The Department may take note
of this and take suitable action.
Action Taken
Noted. The importance of peer learning has been discussed in National Workshops on
quality as an integral part of children centric pedagogical practices.
Initiatives towards Girls Education under SSA/RTE
Recommendations/observations
3.37 Bridging Gender Gaps has been one of the main thrust areas of the SSA-RTE programme.
It was informed that there were 36 districts where gender gap in enrolment was 10 per cent at
primary level and 20 per cent at upper primary level. The maximum number of these districts were
in Punjab (18) followed by Haryana (9), Rajasthan (4), Gujarat, Jammu and Kashmir (2 each) and
Mizoram (1). Specific interventions towards girl education under SSA-RTE include provisions for
KGBVs at upper primary level, activities under NPEGEL, provision of separate toilets for girls,
teacher sensitization programmes to promote equitable learning opportunities for girls, increased
number of women teachers etc.
2

3
Action Taken
Further expansion of KGBVs and NPEGEL will be considered in the 12th Five Year Plan.
The National Programme for Education of Girls at Elementary Level (NPEGEL)
Recommendations/observations
3.39 NPEGEL is implemented in Educationally Backward Blocks (EEB) and addresses the needs
of girls who are in as well as out of school. It also reaches out to the girls who are enrolled in
school but do not attend school regularly. NPEGEL places responsibilities on the teachers to
recognize vulnerable girls, provide them with support services and prevent them from dropping out.
The programme ensures targeted resources through a variety of strategies i.e. girls’ toilets,
bicycles, bridge courses, gender sensitization of teachers etc. The programme works through
village level women and community groups. At present, the programme covers 1.85 crore girls in
430 districts with 40733 model cluster schools. Under the programme 24538 additional classrooms,
21464 girls toilets and 20,520 drinking water facilities have been provided. Besides, 4367 ECCE
centres are also operational covering 92523 children under the scheme.
Action Taken
Noted.
XIV. CONCLUSION
Recommendations/observations
14.1 The year 2012 would be the beginning year of the Twelfth Five Year Plan. The Committee
observes that the performance of the Department of School Education and Literacy has been
satisfactory during the Eleventh Plan Period. However, there are several challenges that lay ahead
before the Department in the Twelfth Plan. The major being fund constraints. As the Department
has been striving for near universal access to secondary education as well along with
universalization of elementary education through its flagship schemes such as RTE, MDM, RMSA,
funding would remain the most crucial aspect. Besides, coordination with the States/UTs and
creating awareness about its various schemes/programmes, especially awareness about RTE would
require monitoring mechanism on the part of the Department. The Committee hopes that the
Department would be able to overcome these challenges and would implement its schemes/
programmes earnestly during the Twelfth Five Year Plan as well.
Action Taken
The issue of providing enhanced allocation for various programmes and schemes of the
Department has been taken up with the concerned authorities. The Department is committed to take
all the necessary action in close coordination with State Governments/UTs for effective
implementation of the programmes and schemes during the 12th Five Year Plan.

4
4
CHAPTER-II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS, WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES
NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLY
II. BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
Recommendations/observations
2.5 The Committee observes that against the projected requirement of ` 85019.80 crore for the
year 2012-13, the Department has been provided with an allocation of `45969.00 crore only which
comes to around 50 per cent of the actual demand of the Department. Given the fact that the
implementation of SSA-RTE programme and other schemes of the Department require enhanced
allocation of the funds, the Committee is constrained to observe that there has been a wide gap
in demand of the Department and actual allocation. The Committee apprehends that insufficiency
of funds would compel the Department to cut down or withdraw from other schemes, besides
leading to hindrances in the implementation of the SSA-RTE programmes which entails specific
time-frame.
Action Taken
The position stated in this para reflects the position as it stands today. This Department
would need enhanced allocation in the Twelfth Plan particularly for SSA-RTE, RMSA and Model
School Scheme, for effective implementation of these and various other schemes. The matter for
providing enhanced allocation for the Department has been taken up with the concerned authorities.
III. SARV A  SIKSHA ABHIYAN/RIGHT TO EDUCATION
Enrolment, Retention and Dropout
Recommendations/observations
3.19 W ith RTE Act, 2009 envisaging a class I to VIII compulsory cycle of schooling for every
child in the age group of 6-14 years, optimal enrollment and retention are two parameters that
acquire utmost importance. Enrollment and retention of the children in the school were the
objectives of the SSA programme also. For enrolment and retention to remain at optimal levels, it
is necessary that drop out rate be kept at the lowest minimum level. As per the District Information
System for Education (DISE) for the year 2009-10, Gross Elementary Enrollment was 187.8
million. According to the Department, there has been improvement in both Gross and Net
enrollment ratios at both primary and upper primary levels. The DISE data of 2009-10 reveals the
following figures:
Class Gross Enrollment Ratio Net Enrollment Ratio
Primary 115.6% 98.2%
Upper Primary 75.8% 58.2%

5
Action Taken
As per DISE 2010-11, the GER and NER at primary level are 118.6 and 99.8 respectively
and the GER and NER at upper primary level are 81.2 and 61.8 respectively. This represents an
improvement in the situation as compared to 2009-10.
Recommendations/observations
3.20 For the year 2010-11, the District Information System for Education records improvement
in NER at Primary and upper primary level to 99.89 and 61.82 per cent respectively. The
Committee is happy to note that the country is close to achieving the goal of universal access at
the primary level. However, when it comes to upper primary level, both GER and NER show
declining trends and the NER especially comes down, to almost half. On a specific inquiry in this
regard, the Department itself admitted that access to upper primary level remains a challenge, both
in terms of GER and NER. The Department attributed this trend to a number of factors such as
non-availability of a school in neighbourhood, poor school infrastructure, non-availability of
adequate number of teachers, economic deprivation of the families, seasonal migration of the
families and other socio-cultural barriers. Another factor contributing to this was the fact that
different States having different ages for students at entry. It was stated by the Department that
in several States, the upper primary level ends in Class VII whereas in calculating the GER and
NER at national level the child population that it used is of age group 11 to 13 corresponding to
classes VI to VIII. Due to exclusion of class VIII enrollment in calculation of GER and NER, the
value of these indicators get reduced. However, the Department itself admitted that children
dropping out at the primary level have an adverse bearing on the GER and NER at the upper
primary level. The Committee is not convinced by the argument of the Department that the value
of GER and NER gets reduced because class VIII students are not counted in some of the States.
The fact remains that up to class VI, almost half of the students drop out from the schooling
system, thus negativing the near universal access at primary level.
Action Taken
One important reason for low NER at the upper primary level is incomplete information
received from the private schools. The RTE Act requires all the recognized schools to furnish
information asked for by the States, and States are trying to have a complete database on enrolment
in private schools. This will definitely help in getting an authentic picture of NER. Besides, the NER
is further expected to improve with the opening of 8,628 upper primary schools sanctioned up to
2011-12 and 1,613 upper primary schools sanctioned in 2012-13.
The average annual dropout rate at primary level came down to 6.8 in 2010-11 from 9.11
in 2009-10. This could become possible because of the greater availability of schools in the
neighbourhood, improvement in the school infrastructure, reduction in the Pupil Teacher Ratio
(PTR), improvement in the quality of textbooks and classroom processes, child centred incentives
like free textbooks and uniforms and greater focus on involvement of School Management
Committees (SMCs). All these efforts would be continued with greater intensity and sharper focus
on the children belonging to disadvantaged groups and weaker sections.
Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya (KGBV)
Recommendations/observations
3.38 Kasturba Gandhi Balika Vidyalaya is a scheme for setting up residential schools at upper
primary level for girls belonging mainly to SC, ST, OBC and Muslim communities. KGBVs are set

6
up in the areas of scattered habitations where schools are at a great distance posing challenge to
the security of girls. KGBVs mainly reach out to adolescent girls who are unable to go to regular
schools, out of school girls in the 10+ age group who are unable to complete primary school,
younger girls of migratory populations in difficult areas of scattered habitations who do not qualify
for primary/upper primary schools. KGBVs provide for minimum reservation of 75% seats for Girls
from SC, ST, OBC and minorities communities and 25% for girls belonging to below poverty line.
Out of 3600 sanctioned KGBVs, 3435 (95.42%) are reported to be functional as on 31.12.2011.
In the year 2011-12, 31 KGBVs were sanctioned to cover educationally backward blocks in the
country. Maximum number of these KGBVs are to be set up in the States of Assam (20), followed
by Meghalaya (8) and Madhya Pradesh, Sikkim and Tripura (1 each). The maximum number of
remaining KGBVs which are yet to be made functional are in Bihar (76) followed by Haryana (27),
Odisha (11), Karnataka & West Bengal (7 each) and Jammu and Kashmir (4). Around 3.35 lakh
girls are enrolled in KGBVs of which 32% are from SC community, 23% from ST Community,
29% from OBC community 8% from BPL and 8% from minority communities.
Action Taken
Out of 3,600 KGBVs sanctioned up to 2011-12, 3,439 have become operational by March,
2012. The issue of KGBVs yet to be operationalized was discussed comprehensively in the Project
Approval Board meetings and State Education Ministers meeting and it was impressed upon the
States to expedite the operationalisation of all the sanctioned KGBVs including 9 new KGBVs
sanctioned in 2012-13.

Action Taken

For effective implementation of the scheme, the scheme guidelines provide for an extensive

institutes have also been engaged to evaluate the Scheme on bi-annual basis and submit the report

· lack of focus on nutrition;
· lack of social accountability mechanisms and grievances redressal mechanism;
· need for capacity building at all levels to improve the effectiveness of the scheme;
· delay in availability of data for effective management of the scheme as well as lack of
availability of real time data on important indicators such as whether MDM has been
served or not.
Action Taken
The Ministry has been taking these issues very seriously and steps are being taken towards
remedial measures through Information Technology interventions. The Centre for Policy Research
has been assigned a study of the fund flow mechanism in two selected districts each in Uttar
Pradesh and Bihar. The Web portal for Mid Day Meal Scheme has been launched and all the States/
