4.17 Another important aspect highlighted in the CAG Report was significant shortfall 
in growth monitoring of every child at AWC.  It is prescribed that maintenan ce of growth 
chart/card for every child at AWCs for assessing their growth using weight -for-age as an 
indicator.  Children up to the age of three years are to be weighed monthly and children 
between the age of three to six years are to be weighed quarterly .  The growth charts are 
required to be analyzed by Child Development Project Officers/health personnel to 
identify mal-nourished children for taking remedial measures.  33 to 47 per cent children 
were not weighed during 2006 -07 to 2010-11.  Test-check of records revealed a shortfall 
of more than 50 per cent of the eligible beneficiaries  in 11 States/UTs (Arunachal 
Pradesh, Assam, Goa, Jammu & Kashmir, Manipur, Meghalaya, Rajasthan, Uttar 
Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Delhi and Puducherry).  Reasons for such a sho rtfall was that 
growth charts were not provided in many AWCs; growth charts not used in some AWCs; 
lack of adequate training to AWWs affected the growth  chart monitoring; non -
availability of a functional baby weighing machine in many AWCs; growth charts 
maintained at AWCs were not checked by supervisor/CDPOs. 
 
4.18 The Committee believes that the objective of the component of 
Supplementary Nutrition was to make available such nutrition to young children 
which takes care of the problem of malnourishment amo ngst children.  Monitoring 
the growth of children in AWCs becomes important to see how the scheme has 
helped in ameliorating malnourishment and  is striving to make children healthy.  
The Committee would like to emphasize that basic equipment for monitoring  i.e 
growth charts, weighing machines etc need to be made available in all AWCs in the 
country with proper maintenance of records of children as per their age, height and 
weight.  Further, adequate training to AWWs and AWHs is required to be given so 
that they are able to perform their duties effectively.  Checking of the records 
maintained at the AWCs should be undertaken by the Supervisors/CDPOs so as to 
ensure their proper maintenance.   
 
4.19 Attention of the Committee has been drawn to the data given i n the CAG Report 
regarding the number of malnourished children exceeding the 40 per cent in 10 
States/UTs like Andhra Pradesh (49 per cent), Bihar (82 per cent), Haryana (43 per cent), 

Jharkhand (40 per cent), Odisha (50 per cent), Rajasthan (43 per cent),  UP (41 per cent), 
Delhi (50 per cent), Daman & Diu (50 per cent) and Lakshadweep (40 per cent).  Further, 
number of severely malnourished children exceeded one per cent of total weighed 
children in eight States like Bihar (26 per cent), Chhattisgarh (2 pe r cent), Gujarat (5 per 
cent), Karnataka (3 per cent), Madhya Pradesh (2 per cent), Maharashtra (3 per cent), 
Uttarakhand (1 per cent) and West Bengal (4 per cent).  Discrepancy in data on the 
nutritional status amongst children also has been reported in t he CAG Report which is a 
matter of grave concern. 
 
4.20 The Ministry of WCD had submitted to the CAG that discrepancy in data with 
respect to nutritional status was on account of usage of old growth standards in some 
AWCs and new World Health Organisation Child Growth Standards in others, resulting 
in increase/decrease in data over the period.  The Committee is of the view that in such 
a scenario, authentic data regarding the nutritional status of children and 
malnourishment would not be available.  The Com mittee would like to recommend 
that the new standards regarding child growth should be adopted in all AWCs 
across the country so that uniformity in method of retrieving authentic information 
regarding the extent of malnourishment is available.  Moreover, t he Committee 
would like to emphasize on addressing the high level of  malnourishment evident in 
States like Bihar, Odisha, Delhi, Daman & D iu, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, 
Haryana etc.  The Ministry should focus its attention on these States so that 
malnourishment amongst children is wiped out totally.   Concerted efforts need to 
be made at the Ministry's level and the State Level to achieve the objective of having 
healthly children through the ICDS component of supplementary nutrition.  SN 
becomes of immense importance in such States where the number of malnourished 
children is very high.   
 
Availability of Pre-School Education (PSE) Kits and Medicine Kits 
4.21 Under the ICDS Scheme, funds are provided to the States/UTs under ICDS 
(General) in the cost sharing  ratio of 90:10 as grants -in-aid for incurring expenditure on 
various components at approved cost norms.  This included expenditure for providing 

Pre-school Education Kits and Medicine Kits and the cost norm for them was `1000/- per 
AWC per annum for PSE kit and `600/-  for Medicine Kit during the last three years. 
 
4.22 The Committee takes note of the expenditure on PSE Kit and Medicine Kits as 
reported by States/UTs which indicates that expenditure incurred on procurement of these 
kits witnessed a reducti on from `4565.53 lakhs in 2011.11 to `4103.70 lakhs in 2011 -12.  
Data for the year 2012 -13 has not been furnished by the Ministry.  Bihar and Gujarat 
have witnessed sharp decline in the expenditure incurred in 2011 -12 while Uttar Pradesh 
and Assam witnesse d quantum increase in the expenditure incurred for PSE and 
Medicine Kits.   
 
4.23 The Committee has been given to understand that the Ministry has been 
requesting the States/UTs from time to time through letters, review meetings, field visits 
to incur expenditure on all the components under ICDS (General) including PSE Kits and 
Medicine Kits.  Under the guidelines issued on 31.3.11 for five tier Monitoring and 
Review Committee, the State level Committee is required to monitor and review 
procurement and supp ly/availability of essential items to AWCs including Pre -School 
Kits and Medicine Kits also. 
 
4.24 The Committee is unhappy with the data furnished by the Ministry with 
respect to the status of procurement of Medicine and Pre -school Kits in States/UTs.  
Proper information of procurement details and the number of States not making 
available PSE and Medicine Kits have not been furnished by the Ministry.  Data for 
the year 2012 -13 ha s not been furnished at all.  The Committee would like the 
Ministry to update its records with respect to availability of Pre -School Education 
and Medicine Kits in the States/UTs so as to know the exact position as of now of 
this important component of ICDS Scheme. 
 
4.25 Attention of the Committee has been drawn to the CAG Report wh erein it has 
been highlighted that Pre-School Education Kits were not available at 41 to 51 per cent of 
the test-checked AWCs during the period 2006-11.  In Madhya Pradesh, none of the 280 -
checked AWCs provided PSE.  In five of the test -checked States (Bih ar, Jharkhand, 

Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal),  data on beneficiaries of PSE who 
joined mainstream education was not available. In five States (Andhra Pradesh, 
Chhattisgarh, Odisha, Rajasthan and Karnataka), shortfall in the number of child ren who 
actually joined the formal education during 2006 -11 ranged between 7 and 30 per cent.  
Further, many of the States did not maintain data base of the beneficiaries or records in 
connection with PSE.  In the absence of this, the extent of services pr ovided under PSE 
could not be ascertained and also indicated absence of monitoring by the Ministry and the 
States.  Moreover, significant under-spending of funds on procurement of PSE Kits by 20 
States was revealed as per the information found available with the Ministry by the CAG. 
States like Jharkhand, Delhi, Punjab, West Bengal, Goa and Uttrakhand consistently did 
not spend funds on procurement of PSE kits during 2006-11. 
 
4.26 To a specific query about the findings of the CAG Report  regarding non -
availability of PSE Kits in 41 to 51 percent of the test -checked AWCs during 2006 -011, 
the Ministry submitted that the cost of programme components like PSE Kits, Medicine 
Kits, etc. under ICDS (Gen) were not released to States through separate sanctions.    
Rather a consolidated amount was released to States/UTs as ICDS (Gen) in four 
installments.  However, from the year 2012-13, the entire cost of programme components 
i.e., PSE Kits, Medicine Kits, etc. had been included in second quarter's installment to 
enable the States/UTs to make procurement accordingly, instead of procuring these items 
in a staggered manner.  States had expressed procedural/administrative difficulty in 
procurement.  However, the Ministry had emphasized upon the States to improve the 
performance.  With the release of cost of programme component in the second quarter of 
the  year 2012 -13,  it was expected that there would be considerable improvement in 
procurement. 
 
4.27 The Committee would like to emphasize upon the importance of the 
availability of PSE and Medicine Kits in AWCs which introduce the young children 
to non-formal pre-school education through a variety of activities and teaching  and 
provide them medical aid whenever required during their stay in an AWC .  It was 
also to facilitat e the transition of the pre -school children in AWCs to the primary 
school.  The Committee, therefore, feels that adequate attention and priority is not 
being given to this component of the ICDS Scheme as most of the States have under -

utilized funds for procurement of such kits.  Adequate attention needs to be given to 
maintaining proper data base of the procurement of kits, number of beneficiaries 
and the number of children moving on from pre -schooling in an AWC to proper 
primary schooling.  Efforts should be made to remove all administrative and 
procedural difficulties faced by the States so as to ensure timely procurement of 
PSE and Medicine Kits for AWCs.

4.29 Committee's attention has been drawn to the findings of the CAG Report on the 
vacancy position of ICDS functionaries.  The Report categorically states that the 
State/UT Governments failed to recruit ICDS staff contemporaneously with th e 
expansion of the Scheme.  The vacancy position against the sanctioned strength had 
declined slightly by the 31 st March, 2011.  However, substantial number of ICDS staff 
was still required to be recruited/engaged in all the four cadres.  The consistent ab sence 
of critical staff at operational projects indicated that the expansion of ICDS to more and 
more new areas was ineffective.  The delivery of services under the scheme had one -to-
one concordance with the availability of critical service -providers.  How ever, the same 
was not ensured by the Ministry at every operational project and the AWC.  Further, the 
Ministry failed to ensure the availability of manpower such as CDPOs and AWWs before 
planning for expansion of the scheme.  The deployment of personnel r emained low in the 
operational projects and AWCs during the period 2006 -11.  Further, test check at District 
Programme Offices and Projects revealed that a large number of DPOs and Projects were 
functioning without essential administrative staff during 200 6-11, despite havings 
sanctioned posts.  The absence of necessary staff adversely affected the administration, 
monitoring and supervision of the Scheme.   
 
4.30 The Committee has been given to understand by the Ministry that since the 
Scheme was implemented by the States/UTs, recruitment to various posts of Supervisors 
and other ICDS functionaries was also done by the States/UTs.  However, the Ministry 
had been regularly taking up the issue relating to filling up of vacancies at various levels 
under the ICD S Scheme with the States in review meetings.  Also, there was not much 
additional financial burden on State Governments in filling up of these vacancies since 
Central Government provided 90 per cent of the expenditure involved under ICDS 
(General).  The Minister, MWCD had taken up with all the CMs of States for expeditious 
filling up of these vacancies vide her letter dated the 18 th July, 2012.  Secretary, MWCD 
had also taken up the matter with States/UTs through letter dated the 5 th September, 2012 
and review meeting on the 13 -14th September, 2012. The Ministry submitted that even 
though ICDS Scheme was a Centrally Sponsored Scheme implemented across the 
country, micro-management at the central level was not feasible.  The Government had 
introduced a five -tier monitoring and supervision mechanism at all levels including 

District and State level with specific responsibility to review vacancy position at all 
levels under ICDS Scheme in the States and to take corrective measures.  The Ministry 
has stressed upon the fact that it had been consistently impressing upon the States to have 
a separate cadre for the ICDS staff.  Under the restructured ICDS, it had been approved 
inter alia that States should create a separate cadre for ICDS functionaries. 
 
4.31 The Committee is highly dissatisfied with the admission of the Ministry that 
micro-management of the ICDS Scheme  in  the context of the issue of vacancies of 
ICDS functionaries was not possible at the level of the Ministry.  Despite other 
efforts of the Ministry, t he crucial problem of vacant positions of key ICDS 
functionaries of AWWs, AWHs, Supervisors and CDPOs continues to persist which, 
to a large extent, adversely affects the delivery of services in an AWC.  Not just this, 
considering the expansion and univers alization of the ICDS Scheme with no 
attention being given to adequate manpower to make A WCs functional seems to be 
a half -hearted measure of expansion of the Scheme in the real sense.  The 
Committee hopes that the Ministry considers the problem of vacant positions of 
ICDS functionaries seriously and address es the same in consultation and co -
operation with the State Governments. 
 
4.32 The Committee would also like to emphasize that the initiative of the 
Ministry regarding having a separate cadre for ICDS st aff is indeed a welcome step 
in the right direction.  However, the Ministry's job is not over with just impressing 
the State Governments to do so.  The Committee feels that since the Central 
Government is giving 90 per cent of the funds to the ICDS (General), it also needs to 
make it mandatory for all the States to have a separate and proper cadre for ICDS 
functionaries.  The norms for recruitment and structure of a separate cadre needs to 
be formulated for tackling the problem of shortage of staff in ICDS.   By doing so, 
the role of the ICDS functionaries would assume great importance and many people 
would look forward to a career working as one of the key functionaries of the ICDS 
Scheme.  The Committee would like to point out that the restructured and 
strengthened ICDS Scheme must focus on having the adequate manpower in AWCs 

across the country with sufficient staff and functionaries at the block and district 
level too for effective maintenance of data and monitoring. 
 
Role and responsibility and training of AWWs 
 
4.33 The Committee observes that there are manifold roles and responsibilities of 
AWWs which are as follows :- 
 To elicit community support and participation in running the programme. 
 To weigh each child every month, record the weight graphically on  the growth 
card, use referral card for referring cases of mothers/children to the sub -
centres/PHC etc., and maintain child cards for children below 6 years and produce 
these cards before visiting medical and para-medical personnel. 
 To carry out a quick su rvey of all the families, especially mothers and children in 
those families in their respective area of work once in a year. 
 To organize non-formal pre-school activities in the Anganwadi of children in the 
age group 3-6 years of age and to help in designin g and making of toys and play 
equipment of indigenous origin for use in anganwadi. 
 To organize supplementary nutrition feeding for children (0 -6 years) and 
expectant and nursing mothers by planning the many based on locally available 
food and local recipes. 
 T provide health and nutrition education and counseling on breast feeding/infant 
& young feeding practices to mothers.  Anganwadi Workers, being close to the 
local community, can motivate married women to adopt family planning/birth 
control measures. 
 To help and coordinate the pregnant and lactating mothers visiting the center to 
get the birth of their child registered and share the information with the village 
level functionary who has been notified as Registrar of Births. 
 To make home visits for educati ng parents to enable mothers to plan an effective 
role in the child's growth and development with special emphasis on new born 
child. 
 To maintain files and records as prescribed. 
 To assist the PHC staff in the implementation of health component of the 
programme viz. immunization, health check -up, ante natal and post natal check 
etc. 
 To assist ANM in the administration of IFA and Vitamin A by keeping stock of 
the two medicines in the centre without maintaining stock register as it would add 
to her administra tive work which would effect her main functions under the 
Scheme. 
 To share information collected under ICDS Scheme with the ANM.  However, 
ANM will not solely rely upon the information obtained from the records of 
AWW. 
 To bring to the notice of the Supervi sors/CDPO any development in the village 
which requires their attention and intervention, particularly in regard to the work 
of the coordinating arrangements with different departments. 

 To maintain liaison with other institutions (Mahila Mandals) and invol ve lady 
school teachers and girls of the primary/middle schools in the village which have 
relevance to her functions. 
 To guide Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHA) engaged under National 
Rural Health Mission in the delivery of health care services and  maintenance of 
records under the ICDS Scheme. 
 To assist in implementation of Kishori Shakti Yojana (KSY) and motivate and 
educate the adolescent girls and their parents and community in general by 
organizing social awareness programmes/campaigns etc. 
 AWW would also assist in implementation of Nutrition Programme for 
Adolescent Girls (NPAG) as per the guidelines of the Scheme and maintain such 
record as prescribed under the NPAG. 
 Anganwadi Worker can function as depot holder for RCH Kit/contraceptives and 
disposable delivery kits.  However, actual distribution of delivery kits or 
administration of drugs, other than OTC (Over the Counter) drugs would actually 
be carried out by the ANM or ASHA as decided by the Ministry of Health and 
Family Welfare. 
 To identify the disability among children during her home visits and refer the case 
immediately to the nearest PHC or District Disability Rehabilitation Centre. 
 To support in organizing Pulse Polio Immunization (PPI) drives. 
 To inform the ANM in case of emergency cases like diahorrea, cholera etc. 
 
4.34 The Committee observes that Anganwadi Workers are matriculate women 
from the local community who come forward to render their services on part -time 
basis.  Being honorary workers, they are paid a monthly honorarium of  `2500.00 
and the benefits like pension, gratuity and other allowances are not applicable to 
them.  They do not have any fixed tenure of service, with only the age of their 
disengagement being fixed at maximum 65 years.  However, they are expected to be 
a multi-tasking expert, being assigned as many as 22 duties, with many of them 
being wide -ranging.  The duties of an Anganwadi Woker as enumerated above 
indicate that not only is she supposed to carry out AWC -specific duties but is also 
expected to make home -visits, maintain a variety of records meticulously.  She is 
also mandated to assist the PHC Staff, ANM, to guide ASHA, to maintain liaison 
with Mahila Mandals, lady school teachers and girls of primary/middle schools, to 
assist in the implementation of Ki shori Shakti Yojana, Nutrition Programme for 
Adolescent Girls, to assist in Pulse Polio Drives and lastly to be in touch with her 
supervisors.    
 

4.35 Nobody can deny the fact that if an Anganwadi Worker has to carry out all 
the assigned tasks with a full  sense of sincerity and strictly in accordance with the 
objective behind each and every task, then it cannot be humanely possible, that too 
for a single woman, having minimum qualification and having her family -specific 
responsibilities, that too on  a part-time basis. One must also not forget that she has  
to work in a society  having population of mainly from illiterate background and 
governed by community specific limitations. 
 
4.36 The Committee also finds that there is an element of overlapping and 
duplicacy if one looks at the duties assigned to ASHA vis -à-vis to those assigned to 
AWW.  Committee's attention has also been drawn towards  the CAG Report which 
mentions about AWWs being engaged in State -specific scheme s also.  The 
Committee has been consistent ly voicing its concern on this crucial issue.  But it 
seems that the Ministry is not inclined to address this problem -area.  The 
Committee can only say that an AWW is the most crucial functionary of ICDS 
Scheme, the Flagship Scheme of the Ministry on which  the entire planning for child 
welfare and development is based. The Committee, therefore,  is of the firm  view 
that an assessment of the roles and responsibilities of AWWs needs to be done to 
rationalize their work , commensurate with resources at their d isposal, training 
provided to them and the honorarium given to them.   
 
4.37 Committee's attention has also been drawn to the following very pertinent 
observations made in the CAG Report on the lack of action on the part of test -checked 
States with regard to applicability of Government of India policy towards improving 
working conditions of AWWs/AWHs:- 
 AWW/AWH Welfare Fund was not created in 10 test checked States (Andhra 
Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Haryana, Jharkhand, MP, Meghalaya, Karnataka, Odisha, 
U.P and West Bengal). 
 A Scheme introduced in December, 2008 to annually provide two sarees was not 
introduced in Madhya Pradesh, Meghalaya and West Bengal.  In Rajasthan, one 
saree was provided during 2010-11 against the norm of two sarees. 
 Disbursement of honorari um for AWWs/AWHs was not regular in six States 
(Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Odisha, Rajasthan and U.P.)   At times, it was 
distursed bi-monthly, quarterly and even half-yearly. 
 As per the Ministry's instructions (August, 2000), a grievance redressal 
Committee was to be set up at district and State levels with representation of 
AWWs and AWHs.  No such Committee was set up in Andhra Pradesh, Gujarat 

and Jharkhand till April, 2011.  No information regarding setting up of the 
Committee was received from Kar nataka, Megahlaya and West Bengal.  
Information on deliberations of the Committee was not available in Chhattisgarh, 
Haryana and U.P.  
 
4.38 The Committee is deeply disturbed by the level of inaction on the part of test-
checked State Governments in providi ng minimum facilities that too funded by the 
Central Government to AWWs/AWHs, the real strength behind effective delivery of 
various services under the ICDS Scheme.  These facilities, inspite of being very 
small initiatives, would have gone a long way in i mproving the quality of life of 
common women folk living in our villages.  It is indeed a sad state of affairs.  The 
Committee has very serious doubts about the status of remaining States of the 
country.  The Committee can only emphasize that all the drawb acks pointed out by 
CAG with regard to service  conditions of AWWs in the test -checked States need to 
be looked into on top priority.  At the same time, the Ministry should also make an 
assessment about the situation prevailing in other States through its w ell-structured 
Central Monitoring Unit.

responsibilities would suffer to a great extent whether it is at the Anganwadi level

Awards to Anganwadi Workers 
 

4.46 As per the ICDS guidelines, in order to appreciate commendable services of 
AWWs, annual National and State level cash awards along with citation were instituted 
from 2000 -01.  The  Committee has been commenting on the unduly long time being 
taken in giving of awards to AWWs. 
 
4.47 As per the latest information given by the Ministry, nominations for national 
level awards to AWWs for 2006 -07, 2007-08 and 2008 -09 have been finalized.  The 
Committee finds it quite disturbing that these awards are yet to be given to the 
selected AWWs.  The meeting of the Selection Committee for National Awards for 
the years 2009-10 and 2010-11 was held on the 19 th March, 2013.  The Committee is 
not aware whether any final decision has been taken by the Selection Committee.  
Awards for 2004 -06 could be given only in February, 2009.  One can imagine the 
time likely to be taken for giving of Awards for later years.   The Committee finds 
that the scheme of Nati onal Awards for AWWs is perhaps going against its very 
objective of motivating AWWs.  What is more disturbing is that there is a question 
mark on the continuation of the Scheme for 2011 -12 and 2012 -13.  The Committee 
finds that even CAG has also expressed its strong reservation on the unduly long 
time being taken in the giving of awards to AWWs.    The Committee  also observes 
that as per CAG Report,  some of the test -checked States were also found lacking in 
implementing this award Scheme  at the State level .  The Committee apprehends 
that the position may be more or less similar in other States.  The Committee 
strongly recommends that the Award Scheme for  AWWs at the national level as 
well as the State level should be continued.  Award money of  `5,000 at the  State 
level and  `25,000 at the national level cannot be  considered a big amount that too 
for a Flagship Scheme like ICDS Scheme having massive financial assistance.  The 
real motivation for an AWW is the recognition being given to her services.  
 
Financial Management of ICDS Scheme 
 
4.48 The Committee takes note of very serious findings of CAG with regard to 
financial management of ICDS.  The first shortcoming relates to unrealistic budgeting for 
payment of salaries.  It was reported that during the peri od 2008-11, a sum of `1,753.00 

crore was released towards the salaries of staff in State Cells, District Cells and Projects 
against which the states reported utilization of `2,853.00 crore.  The actual expenditure 
exceeded the funds released by the Ministr y on salary component to the States by 45 to 
77 per cent.  This happened despite the fact that out of the sanctioned posts for the 
operational projects, 20 to 40 per cent posts were lying vacant.  The Ministry, while 
attributing revision in the pay scales due to the Sixth Pay Commission recommendations 
behind such a situation, also mentioned that in order to meet the shortage  of funds under 
salary, the State Governments directed the funds released to them for other components 
such as procurement of Medicine Kits and PSE Kits, a IEC and flexi-funds for AWCs. 
 
4.49 Another area of concern pointed out by the CAG was unspent balances not 
accounted for.  Unspent balances of the previous year available with the States were not 
taken into account correctly by the Ministry while releasing funds for the subsequent 
year.  This led to excess release of funds to Jharknand ( `13.64 crore in 2011 -12) and to 
Haryana (`11.15 crore in 2009-10). 
 
4.50 CAG also pointed out that test check of annual Statements of Expenditure for  the 
years 2006 -11 available at the Ministry revealed that Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and 
Tamil Nadu claimed excess expenditure amounting to `37.53 crore on account of setting 
up of additional projects and AWCs beyond the norms.  Diversion of funds was also 
reported by some States.  In Haryana, `38.60 crore received for Supplementary Nutrition 
was directed during 2006-11 to Ladli Scheme, Payment of honorarium of AWWs/AWHs 
and for purchase of furniture for new AWCs.  In UP, during 2008 -09, `1.00 crore 
received for IEC activities was diverted to the State sponsored Scheme, Mahamaya Garib 
Balika Ashirwad Yojana.  `6.08 crore received for IEC activities during 2010 -11 was 
diverted for purchase of computers for DPO/CDPO offices.  In Odisha, during 2006 -10, 
`1.41 cr ore was diverted for various purposes like payment of pension, vehicle hire 
charges etc.  In Karnataka, `1.10 crore was diverted during 2006 -11 by CDPO/Deputy 

Directors in three districts for purchase of furniture and payment of salary of ICDS staff 
working in Zilla Panchayat.  In Rajasthan, `9.63 crore received during 2008 -09 for 
payment of arrears of honorarium was diverted to other items of ICDS.  In five Sample 
States, funds amounting to `70.11 crore, i.e in M.P ( `16.87 crore), U.P ( `29.91 crore), 
Bihar (`21.16 crore), Jharkhand ( `3.63 crore) and Andhra Pradesh ( `15.21 crore) were 
retained in Civil Deposits/Personal Ledger Accounts/Bank Accounts/Treasury Accounts. 
 
4.51 The Committee observes that financial discrepancies pointed out by CAG in 
its Report need very serious introspection by all concerned.  These shortfalls 
indicate non-adherence to basic financial norms by the State Governments.  It is all 
the more worrisome that these deviations continued for a long time and went simply 
unnoticed.  Had CAG not undertaken the audit of selected States, these deviations 
might have continued for years.  Funds involved even now are considerably high.  
One can imagine the gravity of such diversion going unabated.  This speaks volumes 
about the non -efficacy of acco unting system at the State level and sheer lack of 
monitoring at the Central level.  It seems nobody is seriously concerned about loss of 
public funds involved.  CAG findings about the basic components of ICDS Scheme 
not being judiciously administered also  equally deserve attention of both the State 
authorities as well as the nodal Ministry at the Centre.   
 
4.52 The Committee observes that as pointed out by CAG, the Central 
Monitoring Unit under the ICDS Scheme failed to efficiently carry out the assigned 
tasks.  The Committee finds the response of the Ministry totally unacceptable.  As 
per the Ministry, immediately after operationalisation of CMU in 2008, NCAER 
started the work of national evaluation of IC DS Scheme entrusted by the Planning 
Commission and the report was submitted in December, 2010.  There was no point 
to duplicate the efforts of assessing the outcomes of ICDS by CMU as well as by 
NCAER.  The Committee is not aware about the findings of NCAER. However, 
nobody would dispute the fact that find ings of CAG, with a focus on financial 
discrepancies and a general evaluation by NCAER commissioned by the Planning 
Commission from the point of view of restructuring of ICDS cannot be equated. 

 
 
V. INTEGRATED CHILD PROTECTION SCHEME (ICPS) 
 
5.1 ICPS is a Cent rally Sponsored Scheme with a view to create a safe and secure 
environment for comprehensive development of children who are in need of care and 
protection, children in conflict with law and other vulnerable children.  The Scheme is 
being implemented from financial year 2009 -10 mainly through the State 
Governments/UT Administrations.  The Scheme has brought several child related 
schemes under one umbrella and also initiated new interventions.  The schemes brought 
within this umbrella scheme are Programme fo r Juvenile Justice, Integrated Programme 
for Street Children and Scheme for Assistance to Homes (Shishu greh) to promote in -
country adoption.  To encourage quicker establishment and procedures under the JJ Act, 
the Ministry introduced the ICPS Scheme for providing financial and technical support to 
the States/UTs.   
 
5.2 The Report of the Working Group on Child Rights for the Twelfth Plan gave a 
situational analysis of children and estimated that around 172 million or 40 per cent of 
India's children were vu lnerable to or experienced difficult circumstances. The major 
highlights of children in conflict with law, children in need of care and protection, 
children living on streets, etc are as given below:- 
 
- Increasing incidences of juvenile crimes from 1999 to 2009.  Under IPC 
crimes, the highest numbers of apprehensions were for theft (6540), hurt 
(4386), burglary (3210) and riots (2025).  These constituted 55.8 per cent of 
the reasons for children being in conflict with law under IPC. 
- Crime committed by childr en under special and local law included highest 
number of juveniles arrested under the Gambling Act (1216), Excise Act 
(613), Prohibition Act (476) and Arms Act (234).  These accounted for 54.4 
per cent of total juveniles arrested 
- Children in need of care and protection as 12.6 million child labourers in the 
age group of 5 -14 in hazardous occupations as per 2001 census.  As per a 
survey by NSSO, the number of working children was reported as 9.075 
million in 2004-05. 
- A study 'surviving the streets' (2011) o n children living on the streets in nine 
districts in Delhi found that there were 27.91 per cent of street living children, 
29.05 per cent of street -working children and 36.03 per cent of those from 
street families.  Nearly one per cent of the total number  of children in Delhi 
were living and working on the streets.  67.3 per cent children felt that they 
were in danger on the streets, 22 per cent children reported being dependent 
on some form of substance of which nearly 50 per cent were daily consumers. 

- Crimes against children increased by 18.57 per cent between 2007 and 2009 
as reflected in Crimes in India 2009.  The increase is attributed to an increase 
in kidnapping and abduction, infanticide, rape and murder during the period. 
- Child Abuse rampant in all  States.  Findings of the Child Abuse study by the 
Ministry in 2007 indicated that in States of Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, 
Delhi, Goa, Gujarat, Kerala, M.P., Maharashtra, Mizoram, Rajasthan, UP, 
West Bengal, 68.99 per cent of children reported physical abuse in one or 
more situations, 20.90 per cent reputed one or more forms of severe sexual 
abuse, 50.76 per cent reported one or more forms of other sexual abuse, 48.37 
per cent reported one or more forms of emotional abuse and 70.57 per cent 
girl children facing one or more forms of neglect. 
 
5.3 Given the kind of data about the children in difficult circumstances and 
facing several forms of abuse and exploitation, the Committee firmly believes that 
the ICPS Scheme is of immense importance in providing a k ind of protective 
network across the country for such children.  Not just this, awareness, 
understanding and sensitivity were  required to address the grappling situations in 
which children found themselves to be in and a way out for their proper 
rehabilitation and care.  The Committee believes that the vulnerable plight of 
children in difficult situations makes the Scheme a crucial one to implement the JJ 
Act across the country through a dedicated structure working to ensure a safe and 
secure environment for children.

5.5 The Co mmittee finds that the ICPS Scheme has slowly picked up pace with 
increasing utilization of allocated funds and the number of beneficiaries, the exception 
being the year 2011-12 when the number of beneficiaries decreased in comparison to the 
previous year.  The Committee also notes that there was a sharp decline in allocation for 

the Scheme from `360.00 crore as in BE 2012 -13 to `233.86 crore as in RE 2012 -13.  
Reasons given by the Ministry for the decrease at the RE stage was that there was delay 
in appoin tment of staff in service delivery structures under ICPS which was not 
anticipated at the time of projecting requirement of funds which resulted in non -
utilization of grants.  In case of four States, namely, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, 
Jharkhand and Sikkim, the State Governments could not release grants to the State Child 
Protection Societies resulting in non -utilization of grants released to these States.  
Consequently, grant released to these four States during previous financial years had been 
revalidated to be utilized during the current financial year.  Further, non -receipt/delay in 
receiving complete financial proposals including timely proposals for the second 
installment of 2012-13 from State/UT Administration was another reason for reduction of 
allocation for the scheme at the RE stage.  
 
5.6 The Committee has been given to understand that all the States/UTs except 
Jammu & Kashmir have signed the MOU for implementation of the scheme.  So far, 619 
Child Welfare Committees, 608 Juvenile Justice Boards, 1 72 Open Shelters, 232 
Specialized Adoption Agencies and 269 Childline Locations have been set up under 
ICPS.  State Child Protection Societies (SCPS) have been set up in 32 States/UTs so  far 
along with District Child Protection Units (DCPUs) in 587 distri cts of the country.  With 
respect to recruitment of staff in State Child Protection Societies, the Committee was 
informed that so far staff had been recruited in SCPS in 12 States/UTs namely, 
Karnataka, Assam, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Nagaland, Gujarat,  Maharashtra, 
Mizoram, Haryana Odisha , Puducherry and Meghlaya. 
 
5.7 The Committee observes that reduction of allocation for the ICPS Scheme at 
the RE stage during the last four years was mainly due to absence of necessary 
structures and staff as their re cruitment was still under process, delay in receiving 
or non-receipt of financial proposals for the Scheme and timely release of funds to 
the SCPSs.  The Committee notes that even though State Child Protection Societies 
had been set up in 32 States/UTs, st aff has been recruited only in 12 States/UTs 
which means that 20 SCPSs are still non -functional.  The Committee believes that 
the setting up of necessary delivery structures  is not adequate enough if required 

manpower to implement the Scheme is not there.  Recruitment of staff for the 
various agencies implementing the Scheme need s to be given the utmost priority for 
effective implementation of the Scheme.  Given the kind of wide network of 
protection envisaged to be given to vulnerable children  under the Sc heme, the 
institutional services, service delivery structures, emergency outreach services, 
Child Tracking system etc have to be in place with required staff to help and 
contribute to the well -being of children in difficult circumstances.  Further, the 
States/UTs need to  be sensitized for sending viable financial proposals on time so 
that utilization of funds is not hindered due to delays etc.   Lastly, the Committee 
feels that the Ministry should approach the State Government of Jammu & 
Kashmir and convince it to sign the MOU for implementation of this Child Welfare 
and protection Scheme. 
 
5.8 Attention of the Committee has been drawn to the following recommendations 
made by the Human Rights Watch titled 'Breaking the Silence; Child Sexual Abuse in 
India:- 
 All child protection homes should be registered with the Government. 
 Relevant laws should be amended to regulate homes and allow penalties on 
defaulters. 
 State Governments should conduct a survey of all residential care facilities and 
provide this informati on to Child Welfare Committees, State Child Rights 
Commissions and the National Commission for the Protection of Child Rights. 
 A monitoring mechanism should be established whereunder children are 
independently interviewed in a safe environment. 
 All institu tions housing children should be subject to regular and periodic 
inspections. 
 
5.9 To a specific query about follow up action on the above recommendations, the 
Ministry submitted that regarding registration of Child Protection Homes, the State 
Governments had been advised from time to time to identify all child care institutions in 
their States/UTs and to ensure that all of these were registered under the JJ Act.  So far, 
25 States/UTs had started the process of identifying and registering child care instit utions 
under the JJ Act.  Also, the JJ Act, 2000 was being reviewed to strengthen the existing 
measures provided for under the Act and, accordingly, various provisions for change 
were under consideration, including those related to registration and punitiv e measures 
for defaulters.  As for survey of all the residential care facilities, State Governments had 

been advised to conduct need assessments at district level under ICPS, including mapping 
of services (such as Homes, Shelters etc) being provided for ch ildren in difficult 
circumstances in each district and also regarding the setting up of Management 
Committees and Children's Committees in every child care institution to supervise the 
functioning of institutions including setting up of complaints and redr essal mechanisms 
wherein the views of children could be shared and recorded for further action.  The JJ Act 
also provided for setting up of Inspection Committee in every State, district and city to 
inter alia visit and oversee the conditions in the institu tions and appropriateness of the 
measures for safety, well-being and permanence available for the children.  15 States had 
set up Inspection Committees so far.  The States were repeatedly being advised to set up 
such Committees expeditiously.   
 
5.10 The Committee is constrained to observe that even after more than ten years 
of the JJ Act coming into force, the mandated bodies to be set up under the Act are 
yet to come up.  The issue of registration of Child Protection Homes under the JJ 
Act is not being pu rsued seriously by the Ministry  as so far , only 25 States have 
started the process of identifying and registering child care institutions.  There is no 
information available regarding the number of such institutions identified and 
registered under the JJ Act in each of these 25 States so far.  Merely advising the 
States to do  so is not enough.  The Committee believes that the Ministry should 
provide a specific time -frame for identifying such child care institutions firstly and 
registering them under the JJ Act subsequently.  The remaining States need to be 
pursued on an urgent basis  to start the over-delayed process of registration of 
institutions.  Further, while information is available about 15 States setting up 
Inspection Committee s, no information is av ailable about the setting up of 
Management Committees and Children's Committee s in child care institutions in 
each State.  The Committee is of the firm view that in the absence of such structures, 
the well -being and protection of children living in such in stitutions cannot be 
ensured.   
 
5.11 The Committee had highlighted the issue of exploitation and abuse of 
children living in orphanages and child care institutions in its earlier Report  also.  

But no significant progress seems to have been made so far.  W ith no designated 
mechanisms in place so far, such institutions have been functioning without any 
supervision or monitoring.  Increasing incidents of child abuse being reported in 
media clearly indicate that in the so called protection homes, the inmates, already 
being victims continue to be exploited, generally in a more organized manner and on 
a regular basis.  The Committee can only say that having well -meaning laws alone 
would not make any change at the ground level.  What is required is their 
implementation in accordance with their objective.  But this can be accomplished 
only through various structures as envisaged in the parent legislation.  The 
Ministry, being the nodal authority for all child -welfare measures has to be pro -
active in sensitizing the State Governments in carrying out their assigned tasks.  
 
5.12 Attention of the Committee has also been drawn to the increasing cases of 
sexual harassment of children in schools where the school management does not 
support the child  victim and his/her pare nts and the child is forced to chan ge the 
school.  The Committee believes that a proper redressal mechanism has to be in 
place in every school of the country for the  harassed child and parents so that strict 
action is taken against the accused and responsi bility of the school management can 
also be fixed. 
 
5.13 Another area of concern which has caught the attention of the Committee is 
the large number of children reported missing, especially in urban areas.  Due to 
delay in reporting and action by concerned  officials, a sizeable number of such 
children remain untraced.  The Committee feels that concerted efforts need to be 
made for tracing missing children so that they are united with their families.  Not 
just this, Ministry of WCD will have to work in activ e co -ordination with the 
Ministry of Home Affairs so as to accord priority to the issue of tracing missing 
children.  It is a critical area of concern as these missing children could be sold, 
trafficked or forced to work as bonded labour.  All sorts of wor se possibilities for 
the missing child can be thought of along with the anxiety and trauma faced by the 
family of the missing child.   
 

5.14 The Committee is happy to note that a beginning has already been made in 
this direction.  The Ministry along with N IC has launched a country -wide training 
programme for police officials and Child Protection Personnel.  Training has been 
conducted in 23 States and 2985 Police Stations have uploaded the data of missing 
and recovered children and 770 Child Care Institutio ns  have uploaded the data of 
children in their care.  The Committee, while welcoming this initiative of the 
Ministry, would like  it to sustain its efforts in sensitizing the remaining States/UTs 
also to come forward and be part of this exercise.  The Committee also observes that 
Childline, a 24 -hour toll free emergency outreach telephone service for children in 
distress is being run by the Ministry through a Mother NGO -Childline India 
Foundation.  Any child requiring assistance can call the service for hel p.  Childline 
personnel provide necessary assistance through linkages with hospitals, Child 
Welfare Committees, Shelter Homes, Police etc.  The Committee notes that this 
service is available in 269 cities in 27 States and 5 UTs.  The Committee welcomes 
these two positive steps taken by the Ministry in co -ordination with other concerned 
agencies.  The Committee, however feels that public at large needs to be made aware 
of these facilities so that more and more number of victims and their families can 
benefit from them.  Services of both print and audio -visual media can easily be 
utilized for this purpose. 
 
5.15 The Committee notes that only 17 States have so far set up State 
Commissions for Protection of Child Rights.  These  States are Assam, Bihar, 
Chhattisgarh, Delhi, Goa, Haryana, Jharkhand, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra, Odisha, Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Tamil Nadu, Uttarakhand and 
West Bengal.  The Ministry had been reminding the remaining State 
Governments/UT Administrations from time to time to set up SCPCR.  The 
Committee would like to point out that the National Commission for Protection of 
Child Rights could be set up in March, 2007 although the Act was enacted in 2005.  
It has taken more than five years for setting up State Commissions in 17 States.  It is 
not known whether the National Commission as well as the State Commissions are 
fully equipped, having the required manpower and infrastructure.  The Committee 
can only say that in view of the vast mandate given to these Commissions, they h ave 

to be functional in the real sense.  The Committee, accordingly, recommends that 
the Ministry has to simultaneously persue with the State Governments for setting up 
of these Commissions and also ensure their being made functional as early as 
possible.    
 
VI. RAJIV GANDHI SCHEME FOR EMPOWERMENT OF ADOLESCENT 
GIRLS (RGSEAG) - SABLA 
 
6.1 SABLA is a comprehensive scheme for the holistic development of adolescent 
girls introduced in the year 2010 by merging the erstwhile Kishori Shakti Yojana (KSY) 
and the Nutrition Programme for Adolescent Girls (NPAG) Scheme.  It is a Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme primarily for out of school adolescent girls (11 -18 years) 
implemented in 200 districts across the country on a pilot basis through the State 
Governments using the ICDS platform.  SABLA is being implemented through  the State 
Governments/UTs with 100 per cent financial assistance from the Central Government 
for all inputs other than nutrition provision for which 50 per cent central assistance is 
provided to States.  Anganwadi Centre is the focal point for the delivery of the services.  
SABLA aims at an all -round development of adolescent girls of 11 -18 years by making 
them self-reliant by facilitating access to learning, health and nutrition through various 
interventions such as health, education, vocational training etc. 
 
6.2 The Scheme has two major components, nutrition and non -nutrition component.  
Under the nutrition component, adolescent girls are provided with Take Home Rations 
(THR) or hot cooked meals as per t he feasibility.  While under the non -nutrition 
component, the girls are provided information on topics like improving the nutritional 
and health status, Family Welfare and Adolescent Reproductive and Sexual Health 
(ARSH).  The Scheme also provides for regu lar health check up, supply of IFA tablets, 
mainstreaming out of  school adolescent girls into school system, life skill education and 
vocational training.  Central Government is providing 100 per cent financial assistance 
for all inputs other than nutriti on.  For nutrition,50 per cent of Central assistance is 
provided to the States/UTs.  The Scheme is likely to cover nearly one crore adolescent 
girls annually.  Till September, 2011, nearly 40 lakh girls have been already benefited 
under the nutrition component of the Scheme.

VII. INDIRA GANDHI MATRITVA SAHYOG YOJANA (IGMSY) 
 
7.1 Indira Gandhi Ma tritva Sahyog Yojana (IGMSY): A Conditional Cash Transfer 
Scheme, a Centrally Sponsored Scheme for pregnant and lactating women was 
introduced in October, 2010 to contribute to a better enabling environment by providing 
cash incentives for improved health and nutrition to pregnant and nursing mothers.  The 
Scheme envisages providing cash to pregnant and lactating (P&L) women during 
pregnancy and lactation in response to individual fulfilling of specific conditions.  It 
addresses short term income support objectives with the long term objective of behavioral 
and attitudinal changes.  The Scheme attempts to partly compensate for wage loss to 
pregnant and lactating women, both prior to and after delivery of the child.  Being 
implemented on pilot basis in 53 sel ected districts using the platform of ICDS, 12.5 lakh 
P&L women are expected to be covered every year under IGMSY.  The beneficiaries are 
paid `4000/- in three installments per P&L woman between the second trimester and till 

the child attains the age of 6 months on fulfilling specific conditions related to maternal 
and child health.  Pregnant women of 19 years of age and above for first two live births 
are eligible under the Scheme.  The modalities of cash transfer are decided by the State 
Government/UTs.  The modes of cash transfer include -nationalized bank, post office, 
cooperative bank, business correspondent model of bank, etc.

7.5 The Committee in its earlier Report had drawn attention to a scheme o f the 
Ministry Health and Family Welfare i.e Janani Suraksha Yojana which was a Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme launched in 2005 with the objective to increase institutional 
deliveries.  The Committee had recommended that a convergence of both the schemes i.e 
IGMSY and Janani Suraksha Yojana may be explored by the Ministry to avoid duplicacy 
and maximize the reach of benefits to the targeted  women.  The logic behind the 
suggestion for any kind of convergence and co -ordination was due to the fact that both 
the schemes were to be handled by AWWs and ANM functionaries of AWCs and PHCs 
respectively. 
 
7.6 The Ministry has submitted that since the objective of both the Schemes was 
different, there was no over -lapping.  Under JSY, a cash incentive was provided for 
pregnant mothers to have institutional births as well as pre and ante -natal care.  The 
Scheme primarily aimed at promoting institutional delivery.  IGMSY, on the other hand, 
provided cash incentives for improved health and nutrition to pregnant and nursing 
women for improving health and nutrition and partially compensate for wage loss.  It was 
also pointed out that there was close convergence of Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare and ICDS at the grass root level which facilitated dissemination of information 
about JSY and IGMSY schemes and availing benefits thereof.   
 
7.7 The Committee is constrained to observe that even though both the schemes, 
JSY and IGMSY cater to the needs of pregnant and nursing mothers, the Ministry 
seems reluctant to explore the possi bility of convergence of the two schemes.  The 
Committee is only making an attempt to highlight the fact that most of Indian 

women, especially those residing in rural areas are in poor state of health and are 
weak and anaemic.  Such women when pregnant nee d all kinds of support and care 
for their well -being during pregnancy and delivery and also during nursing. All 
these aspects concerning their health, nutrition and pre and ante -natal care are 
inter-connected and hence convergence of both the schemes would be desirable. The 
Committee, therefore, would like to reiterate its earlier recommendation and 
request the Ministry to explore the possibility of convergence of the two schemes for 
the well-being of pregnant mothers and avoid any over-lapping.

monitor and regulate in -country and inter-country adoption.  CARA primarily deals with 
adoption of orphan, abandoned and surrendered children through its 
associated/recognized adoption agencies.  It functions as a nodal body on non -
institutional child care services in the country and is envisaged as a central authority 
under the Hague Convention on Inter-country Adoption.

8.5 The Committee has been given to understand that a new adoption regime had 
been initiated by the Government with notification of the 'Guidelines Governing the 
Adoption of Children -2011' and also the implementation of Child Adoption Reso urce 
Information & Guidance System (CARINGS) which aimed at a transparent and friendly 
adoption process.  It offered a more child -centric approach and was an online platform 
which helped in building bridges and creating a link through a robust web -based 
management system.  Its objective was to facilitate expeditious and smooth adoption, 
ensuring transparency in the adoption process by increasing the accountability of 
implementing agencies.  The Ministry, however, submitted that much remained to be 
done as a  large number of waiting parents were there in comparison to less number of 
children available for adoption.  All adoption agencies in the country needed to update 
and upload child specific information online for expeditious adoptions.  Delays had been 
noticed at the level of Child Welfare Committees and the Court granting adoption order 
in each case.  These issues had been taken up separately with the concerned authorities.  
The Ministry further submitted that children homes all over the country needed to be 
connected with adoption agencies to enable expeditious placement of orphan, abandoned 
and surrendered children.  There was a need to stop all adoptions through unauthorized 
individuals and agencies. The waiting period of the prospective parents was beli eved to 
be minimized once more children were available in adoption in agencies. 
 
8.6 The Committee notes that as per the data provided by the Ministry till  the 
31st December, 2012, the number of in -country and inter -country adoptions had 
decreased in the year 2012-13.  The year 2011 -12 saw the total number of adoptions 
(in-country and inter-country) to 6494 whereas the total number in the year 2012-13 
(till 31.12.12) was only 3252.  It was likely to increase but the likelihood of doubling 
the numbers in the matter of three months i.e till March, 2013 seemed difficult to be 
achieved.  The Committee also notes that CARINGS was introduced to make way 
for a smooth and transparent adoption process but as admitted by the Ministry 
itself, a lot more needed to be do ne.  The Committee is of the view that the following  
steps needed to be taken for making the whole process of adoption a much more 
simpler and easier one for prospective parents:- 
 

 Children Homes to be connected directly to the adoption agencies with 
complete information about all the children in their Homes indicating the 
availability of a number of children residing in a Home 
 A maximum time frame need to be specified so that prospective parents have 
a rough idea about the possible time that would be taken  in completing all 
procedures and adopting a child.  
 Delays at the level of Child Welfare Committee and the Court granting 
adoption need to be avoided and a specified time -frame should be specified 
for these agencies too to grant adoption , thereby minimizing the endless wait 
of the prospective parents 
  Check on all adoptions through unauthorized individuals and agencies. 
 Data base of missing children should be circulated amongst all Children 
Homes from time to time to trace missing children if they had some how 
reached in any Home so as to unite them with their parents. 
 
The Committee believes that the hopes and desire of prospective parents should not 
be dashed in view of the complicated adoption procedure and their endless wait for 
adopting a child.  Moreov er, encouraging child and parent friendly procedure 
would help many orphaned, abandoned or surrendered children to find homes and 
families to blossom with warmth and love. 
 
8.7 Committee’s attention has also been drawn to the recommendation of giving 
CARA the status of a statutory structure under the JJ Act made by the Working 
Group on Child Rights for the Twelfth Plan.  The Committee is in agreement with 
the Working Group observation that such a status would result in CARA 
addressing adequately the issues r elated to monitoring, accountability, conflict of 
interest, scrutiny of agencies,data management etc. It is also high time that presence 
of CARA is in all the States. 
 
8.8 Attention of the Committee has been drawn to media reports where cases of 
exploitation of children in inter -country adoptions have been reported.  The Ministry has 
submitted that the guidelines 'Governing the Adoptions of Children 2011'  ensured 
adequate safeguards for children placed in inter -country adoption as provided in the 
Hague Convention on Protection of Children and Cooperation in respect of Inter -country 
Adoption (1993) ratified by GOI.  Each case of inter -country adoption was approved by 
competent authority of the receiving country which was obliged to provide adequate 
safeguard to the adopted children. The progress reports of the children placed in inter -

country adoption were monitored for a period of two years and the child protection 
service of the receiving country took appropriate measures in case of any abuse or 
neglect.  C hildren placed in inter -country adopted were now supported with adoption 
orders under the JJ Act to enable their citizenship expeditiously.  Moreover, amendments 
to the JJ Act were supposed to have a separate chapter on adoption.   
 
8.9 The Committee is re lieved to know that inter -country adoptions with orders 
under the JJ Act enabled the adopted children in expediting their citizenship status.  
However, there are numerous concerns regarding the inter-country adoptions, more 
so because mostly children with special need are being  placed in such adoptions.  
These children, therefore, need  much more protection from abuse and neglect and 
safeguarding of their rights.  The Committee recommends to the Ministry to 
specifically lay down guidelines and norms with res pect to inter -country adoptions 
in the JJ Acts itself as early as possible with strict monitoring provisions to check 
any abuse/neglect of the adopted child.  The Committee also notes that during 2012 -
13, CARA had undertaken inspection of 45 adoption agencies up to December, 2012. 
The Committee would appreciate if such inspections are carried out on a regular 
basis followed by corrective measures. The Committee feels that surprise 
inspections should also be made as real position at the ground level would the n 
emerge. 
 
IX. RASHTRIYA MAHILA KOSH (RMK)

in 1993 for the purpose of providing micro-loans to poor women through government and 
non-government organizations, women federati ons and cooperative banks.  RMK started 
with an initial corpus of `31.00 crore which has grown to `186.00 crore.  RMK extends 
loans through a client -friendly, without collateral and hassle free mechanism for 
livelihoods, micro-enterprises, housing and fami ly needs in both rural and urban areas.  
Apart from giving micro-credit, it also builds the capacities of Self  Help Groups/women 
members and partner organizations through trainings in financial management, enterprise 
development, skills and modern practic es, as well as exposure visits and assistance in 
marketing.

network across the country including the Andaman & Nicobar Islands and the border

repeat loan `50,000 taken together, the existing plus new loan.  The Committee 
strongly feels that a well -structured monitoring mechanism at all level needs to be 
put in place without any further delay.   
  
9.4 The Committee also takes note of the fact that out of `340.13 crore sanctioned 
upto the 15th December, 2012 to different States, the maximum beneficiaries have 
been the States of Andhra Pradesh ( `98.50 crore)  and Tamil Nadu ( `74.91 crore) 
having availed of half of the to tal funds sanctioned (`173.41 crore).  The Comm ittee 
strongly feels that States like U.P, Chhattisgarh, Arunachal Pradesh, Mizoram need 
to be more involved.  Also , uptil now, there has been no participation from Tripura, 
Meghalaya, Goa and Chandigarh.  The Committee would appreciate if the Ministry 
takes up this issue with all the concerned States. 
  
9.5 Details of RMK -NGO Partners provided funds and loan disbursed from the 
1st January, 2012 to the 15th December, 2012 indicated that out of `25.08 crore funds 
provided, loan disbursed amounted to only `13.36 crore.  Out of 41 RMK -NGO 
Partners, there were 17 NGO Partners which although had not been provided funds 
during this period seemed to have disbursed loan, with no  details of beneficiaries 
being available.  Besides that, there were  3 NGO Partners which  neither provided 

funds nor disbursed loans but seemed to have loan beneficiaries.     This clearly 
shows that accounts of funds sanctioned, disbursed and the number of beneficiaries 
are not being maintained as per the prescribed norms.  The Committee would  
appreciate if a proper review of funds sanctioned, disbursed, recovered State wise 
and NGO –wise is undertaken and corrective measures taken accordingly. 
 
9.6 The Committee would like to point out that the modalities for  disbursal of 
loans to women benefi ciaries need to be made transparent and simple.  Apparently, 
the rate of interest at which funds are provided to IMOs and the rate of interest 
charged by IMOs from the beneficiaries are different.  The Committee is of the view 
that there should be minimum gap in the interest rate charged from NGOs and 
beneficiaries.  Also, the rate of interest charged from women beneficiaries should be 
kept at a minimal level so as to avoid  unnecessary burden of them.  The Committee 
feels that the very purpose of the Scheme  would be defeated if the interest rates 
were higher than the market rate which would certainl y discourage the poor and 
asset-less women from availing benefits under the Scheme.  Further, a time period 
needs to be specified for sanctioned but not disbursed loan amount to be returned to 
RMK by the IMOs or the NGO Partners.  This will ultimately result in funds 
reaching the beneficiaries in real need and being assisted by well -performing 
NGOs.. 
 
 
9.7 To a specific query about the status of restructuring of RM K and utilization 
of funds for RMK, the Committee has been given to understand that it was 
proposed to restructure and strengthen RMK from  the existing RMK single office 
society to Government owned Non Deposit Taking Systematically Improvement 
Non-Banking Finance Company under Section 617 of the Companies Act, with  a 
Pan India n Office network backed by need -based capital.  This was intended to 
enable RMK to respond to the growing need for micro -finance in low -income 
households on reasonable terms and condi tions and to reach out more effectively to 
poor women in the hither to less-covered or uncovered States/areas.  An EFC note 
dated the 12th August, 2011 was circulated by the Ministry to incorporate a new 
Public Limited Company, namely RMK limited by GOI by infusion of `100.00 crore 

in the first year and capitalized at `500.00 crore by the fifth year.  This was 
considered by EFC in its meeting held on the 18th June, 2012.  The EFC expressed 
concerns on whether the NBFC as proposed would be financially indepen dent as 
restructuring would add to operational costs; whether the proposed NBFC would 
access funds from the market and if so at what point and in what form; whether on 
dissolution of the Society, the funds in its accounts could be transferred to NBFC 
instead of being returned to Government account and also whether the entire 
business of the Society, including doubtful debts, decreed cases etc. could be taken 
over by NBFC.    In view of  the above, opinion of Attorney General through  the 
Ministry of Law on th e legal issue involved in the dissolution of RMK as a Society 
and transfer of its business to the proposed NBFC, was requested by this Ministry 
vide D.O. letter dated the 31st July, 2012.  The opinion/advice of the Department of 
Legal Affairs/Ld. Attorney General in the matter was awaited.  Hence, in the 
absence of approval of competent authority, expected expenditure of `100.00 crore 
(including `10.00 crore under NE) for incorporation of RMK Limited could not be 
made.  A sum of `20.00 crore (including `2.00 crore under NE) has been kept in BE 
2013-14 for incorporation of RMK Limited. 
  
9.8 The Committee takes a serious view of nil utilization of funds for RMK since 
the last three years due to the restructuring exercise of RMK which has yet not got 
the neces sary approvals.  The whole process of seeking approval for the 
restructuring exercise is moving at a snail's pace leading to no sanctioning of funds 
to States/UTs and nil performance of the scheme during the last three years.  The 
Committee can only hope t hat the restructuring exercise is expedited by the 
Ministry after seeking the necessary approvals so that women beneficiaries benefit 
from the restructured scheme with new components. 
  
X. HOSTELS FOR WORKING WOMEN 
 
10.1 The Scheme of Hostel for Working Wo men envisages provision of safe and 
affordable hostel accommodation to working, single working women, women working at 

places away from their home -town and for women being trained for employment.  Since 
its inception in 1972 -73, 902 working women hostels h ad been sanctioned under the 
Scheme all over the country, benefitting about 67,284 working women.  One new hostel 
had been sanctioned in rented premises benefitting 25 working women.   The Scheme has 
been revised with following salient features:- 
 Financial assistance for construction of hostel building to be given only on public 
land. 
 Financial assistance available for rent of the hostels run in rented premises also. 
 Provision for maintenance grant of hostel building (maximum `5.00 lakh) and 
one-time non-recurring grant for furnishings @ `7500/- per beneficiary. 
 State Government agencies, Urban Municipal Bodies, Cantonment Boards, Civil 
Society Organizations, Panchayati Raj Institutions, Self Help Groups, recognized 
College/Universities and Corporate associa tions like CII, ASSOCHAM and 
FICCI included under the revised Scheme. 
 
The State Governments had been advised to disseminate the revised guidelines of the 
Scheme and send project proposals accordingly.   
 
10.2 In the year 2012 -13, `9.00 crore was allocated  for the Scheme at the BE stage 
which was reduced to `7.47 crore at the RE stage.  Out of this, `5.75 crore had been 
released up to February, 2013 for the construction of working women's hostels across the 
country.  The Committee has been given to understa nd that due to non -receipt of 
complete and viable proposals from State Governments, only 12 projects were sanctioned 
during 2012-13 resulting in less utilization of grants/reduced RE.  State Governments had 
been advised to forward proposals after making ne ed-based demand survey for Working 
Women's Hostel.  The State Governments were reminded on the 19 th January, 2011 to 
expedite the demand surveys and send proposals as per the schematic norms of the 
revised Scheme. 
 
10.3 The Committee is of the view that th e revision of the Scheme has not helped 
in the performance of the Scheme with respect to the receipt of complete and viable 
proposals for construction of new hostels for working women.  In the year 2011, 
only one proposal was received , while 12 proposals h ad been sanctioned in the year 
2012-13.  The possibility of not getting viable and complete proposals due to revised 

norm of having public land for the construction of hostels was highlighted by the 
Committee and the Ministry had also admitted to the same and had decided to re -
consider its decision to allow construction only on public land.  However, nothing in 
this regard had been done by the Ministry in the past year 2012 -13, which has led to 
a discouraging response leading to non -receipt of viable propos als under the 
Scheme.   
 
10.4 The Committee is of the view that  the Ministry needs to assess the 
implications of the revised norms of the Scheme and take corrective measures to 
improve the performance of the Scheme with respect to construction of more host els 
for working women.  Views of the State Governments , especially the bottlenecks 
faced by them in formulation of viable proposals needed to be obtained. Result of 
need based demand surveys and feed back of the State Governments should be used 
by the Minis try to understand the practical problems faced by the States/UTs 
Further, the Committee had suggested to the Ministry to explore the possibility of 
Public-Private Partnership model in the construction of hostels for women.  The 
Committee would like to reiterate that the Ministry should explore the possibility of 
using the PPP model in the scheme for provision of many more number of hostels 
for the benefit of working women.   
 
XI. SWADHAR GREH 
 
11.1 The Scheme of Swadhar Greh is meant to reach out to those w omen who are 
victims of unfortunate circumstances and are in need of institutional support for 
rehabilitation.  The Committee observes that funds allocated for this Scheme during 
2012-13 remained under –utilised.  On a specific query in this regard, the 
Committee was informed that the new Swadhar Greh Scheme, which was 
formulated by merging the existing Swadhar and Short Stay Home Schemes, would 
be operational during the year 2012 -13.  Accordingly, an enhanced allocation of 
`90.00 crore was kept in BE 2012 -13 for release of funds to the implementing 
agencies at the improved, revised rate.  However, due to the new Scheme not getting 
all the necessary approvals, it could not be implemented as per the existing financial 
norms and allocated funds had to be reduc ed at the RE stage.  The Committee 

observes that even the reduced funds remained under -utilised.  The Committee has 
been given to understand that with an allocation of `75.00 crore for 2013 -14, all 
suitable Swadhar Homes/Short Stay Homes are envisaged to b e converted into 
Swadhar Greh and funds will be released with increased financial norms.  More 
Swadhar Greh will be set up in uncovered districts. 
 
11.2 The Committee notes that the exercise of merger of the two Schemes of Short 
Stay Homes and Swadhar Started with an evaluation study conducted by the Centre 
for Market Research and Social Development, New Delhi in 2007.  The study, 
pointing out similarities in the profile of inmates, admission procedures, 
components of the Scheme (counseling, vocational trai ning, rehabilitation) and 
follow-up procedure, recommended merger of both the schemes for better 
functioning and outcomes with lesser administrative burden.   The Committees 
would like to point out that its views and recommendation was also on the same line.  
The Committee, however, is somewhat disturbed by the undue delay taking place.  
It has taken the entire Eleventh Plan period and one year of the Twelfth Plan has 
also gone but the process of merger of two Schemes is still continuing. The 
Committee is not aware whether the suitable Short Stay Homes have been identified 
for their being brought under the revised Scheme of Swadhar.  The Committee is of 
the view that thorough review of functional Shelter Homes under both the Schemes 
covering all the aspects -infrastructure, manpower, funds available , both duly 
accounted for and unspent balances and also the problem -areas has to be made, if 
not already initiated and completed at the earliest.   This is all the more required as 
details about Short Stay Homes , allocated funds and number of beneficiaries do not 
match in the details furnished to the Committee in response to its questionnaire and 
those given in the Annual Report of the Ministry.  While as per the Annual Report 
in 2011 -12, 320 SSHs having 19,949 inmate s were released funds, as per the 
Committee Questionnaire, there were 358 SSHs having 21,417 inmates.   The 
Committee also feels that as observed by the Working Group that all the districts 
need to be covered under the Scheme so that women victims of violen ce and 
deserted/separated and destitute women have a place to go in time of need.  The 

Scheme would be better managed if State Women Commissions/State Governments 
are actively involved in the monitoring of Shelter Homes.   
 
XII. NATIONAL MISSION FOR THE EMPOWERMENT OF WOMEN 
 
12.1 The National Mission for Empowerment of Women (NMEW) was launched on 
the 8 th  March, 2010, with a view to empowering women socially, economically and 
educationally.  The Mission aims to achieve empowerment of women on all these fro nts 
by securing convergence of scheme/programmes of different Ministries/Departments of 
Government of India as well as State Governments.  Alongside, the Mission shall 
monitor and review gender budgeting by Ministries/Departments.  NMEW will facilitate 
the processes that ensure holistic empowerment of women with special focus: 
- to ensure economic empowerment of women  
- to ensure that violence against women is eliminated progressively 
- to ensure social empowerment of women with emphasis on health and 
education 
- to oversee gender mainstreaming of programmes, policies of participating 
Ministries and organizations 
- to undertake awareness generation and create, if required, structures at 
district, tehsil and village level with the involvement of Panchayats f or 
their fulfillment. 
 
NMEW has identified a three pronged strategy to achieve its objective of holistic 
empowerment of women through intervention at the policy level by reviewing 
studies/evaluations/impact assessment of programmes/schemes for gender equal ity, 
strengthening the implementation and delivery mechanism and empowering women to 
demand their entitlements.   
 
12.2 The Committee has been given to understand that during 2012 -13, the 
institutional mechanism under the mission was operationalized with t he setting up of the 
National Unit headed by the Additional Secretary and Mission Director.  It also had 
experts in the fields of poverty alleviation, social empowerment, health and nutrition, 
gender budgeting, gender rights and law enforcement, empowermen t of vulnerable and 
marginalized women, media, awareness generation, advocacy and mass communication 
and Information Technology services.  Further, the Central Monitoring Committee 
(CMC) and Inter -Ministerial Co -ordination Committee (IMCC) set up to monito r and 
facilitate convergence across Ministries met during 2012 -13.  Also, 21 States had set up 

the State Resource Centre for Women (SRCW) which operationalizes the activities of the 
Mission.  Poorna Shakti Kendras (PSKs) were to be platform/forum for women  to come 
together and explore their potential and possibilities, raise awareness about their social, 
economic and political rights and facilitate access to schemes and entitlements and build 
capabilities for promoting women's participation in decision -making.  The first such pilot 
project was launched in Pali District, Rajasthan in September, 2011 with a new model of 
delivery i.e the Convergence Model with the opening of 150 village centres.  Apart from 
all this, the Mission conducted conferences, seminars,  events and other research studies 
with the objective of achieving convergence for empowerment of women.   
 
12.3 The Committee notes that the budgetary allocation for NMEW was 22.50 crore 
for the year 2012 -13 which was reduced to `9.90 crore at the RE stag e.  The Ministry 
submitted that due to slow pace of submission of proposals on running of pilot schemes 
for achieving convergence by the States and delay in setting up of State Resource Centres 
for Women, expenditure remained low.  Hence, due to budgetary constraints of the 
Government, the RE figure was brought down in 2012 -13.  However, with the gradual 
progress in setting up of State Resource Centres for Women and progress made in 
initiating pilot schemes both by States, NGOs etc through sustained NMEW, i t was 
envisaged that the Mission could be in a position to achieve substantially increased 
expenditure in the financial year 2013-14.  Therefore, the BE 2013-14 had been increased 
to `49.50 crore.
