III.  HIGHLIGHTS OF WORKING GROUP REPORT ON CHILD RIGHTS
3.1 The Ministry informed that a Working Group on Child Rights was constituted by the
Planning Commission to recommend priorities and strategies for children in the Twelfth Five Year
Plan 2012-2017. It recommended that the Twelfth Plan represent a new “Child Rights Paradigm”
that mandates the fulfillment of children’s rights to survival, development, protection and
participation, as the foundation of human development and as the driver of faster, more inclusive
and sustainable growth. India is home to the largest number of children in the world. 19 per cent
of world’s children live in India. It is estimated that 40 per cent of children are in difficult or
vulnerable circumstances. The Report of the Working Group on Child Rights highlights the
various parameters which underlines the condition of children in India which are mentioned
below:–
● Child sex ratio (0-6 years) as per census 2011 is 914 girls for 1000 boys.
● Child mortality (under 5 mortality rate is 60 per 1000 births for boys and 69 per 1000
births for girls.
● Anaemia among children (6-59 months) is 69.5 per cent and while only 30 per cent of
boys in age-group of 15-19 years are anaemic, 56 per cent of girls in the age-group
of 15-19 years are anaemic.
● Nearly 22 per cent newly born children have Low Birth Weight (LBW) i.e. below
2.5 kgs.
● While 55 per cent of total boys are fully immunized in the age of 12-13 months only
52 per cent of girls are fully immunized.

7
● 54.5 per cent of children (9 months and above) received at least 1 dose of Vitamin-A
supplement.
● 40.5 per cent children Breast fed within 1 hour of birth.
● 47 per cent adolescent girls and 58 per cent adolescent boys of 15-19 years have less
that 18.5 kgs/m 2 of Body Mass Index.
● As per NFHS-3 data, about 11.8 per cent children are found to be engaged in work.
Amongst major States, Gujarat has the highest proportion of children working at 32 per
cent followed by Rajasthan which has 20 per cent working children.
3.2 The Ministry also submitted that an ambitious and well-articulated agenda has been set in
the area of child rights and protection in Eleventh Plan. A process of systematic transformation
towards attainment of the goal of inclusive growth has been initiated and there has been
considerable progress made. However, there is need to strengthen the institutional framework and
administrative machinery for programme/scheme implementation along with clear norms, standards
and guidelines for safeguarding the interests and rights of children. Unmet targets of the Eleventh
Plan in areas of law and scheme implementation related to child protection, malnutrition, child sex
ratio, school drop-out rates and maternal mortality, indicate that there is still a long distance to
cover, to bridge the gap between what was envisioned and what exists as of now.
3.3 Keeping in view of the present position of children in the country, the Committee
believes that efforts are required to ensure that resources are judiciously utilized towards
implementing new schemes and that right preparations should be made for a better and
efficient implementation of these Schemes. There is a need for efforts to provide flexibility
of norms to address critical needs at the community level by creating a flexi-pool of
resources and the need for funding schemes with realistic cost norms. Policy formulation,
strengthening programmes execution, enforcement of laws, plan implementation, capacity-
building and scheme monitoring are some of the areas that need immediate attention and
strengthening. Convergence between various sectoral policies and programmes that impact
the lives of children and inter-sectoral coordination are vital for bridging the shortfalls in
achievements.
IV. INTEGRATED CHILD DEVELOPMENT SERVICES SCHEME (ICDS)
4.1 The Ministry submitted that, for the holistic development of children, it has been
implementing the world’s largest and most unique and outreach programme of Integrated Child
Development Services (ICDS) providing a package of six services comprising
(i) Supplementary nutrition
(ii) Immunization
(iii) Health check-up
(iv) Referral services
(v) Pre-school non-formal education
(vi) Health and Nutrition Education
The Ministry further added that health related services are provided through convergence
with Health Ministry. The ICDS scheme has been universalized with 7076 ICDS Projects and
14 lakh Aanganwadi Centres (AWCs) including Mini AWCs. The scheme presently operates through
a network of about 7067 operational projects and about 13.42 lakh AWCs as on 30.09.2014.

8
4.2 In order to address various programmatic, management and institutional gaps and to meet
administrative and operational challenges, Government approved the proposal for Strengthening and
Restructuring of ICDS Scheme with an over-all budget allocation of `1,23,580 crore during
Twelfth Five Year Plan. The key features of Strengthened and Restructured ICDS inter-alia include
addressing the gaps and challenges with (a) special focus on children under 3 years and pregnant
and lactating mothers (b) strengthening and repackaging of services including care and nutrition
counseling services and care of severely underweight children (c) a provision for an additional
Anganwadi Worker cum Nutrition Counselor for focus on children under 3 years of age and to
improve the family contact, care and nutrition counseling for P&L Mothers in the selected 200
high-burden districts across the country, besides having provision of link worker, 5 per cent crèche
cum Anganwadi centre (d) focus on Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) (e) forging strong
institutional and programmatic convergence particularly, at the district, block and village levels
(f) models providing flexibility at local levels for community participation (g) introduction of APIP
(h) improving Supplementary Nutrition Programme including cost revision (i) provision for
construction and improvement of buildings of Anganwadi centres (j) allocating adequate financial
resources for other components including Monitoring and Management and Information System,
Training and use of Information and Communication Technology (ICT), (k) to put ICDS in a
mission mode etc. and (l) revision of financial norms etc.
4.3 Restructured and Strengthened ICDS has been rolled out in all the districts in three phases
as per following details:
(a) In 200 high burden districts in the first year (2012-13);
(b) In additional 200 districts in second year (2013-14) ( i.e. w.e.f.  01.04.2013) including
districts from special category States and NER;
(c) In remaining districts in third year (2014-15) ( i.e. w.e.f.  01.04.2014).

4.27 The Committee has been informed that the Programme Evaluation Organization of the

Council for Applied Economic Research (NCAER) . The Study covered a sample of 19500
households, 3000 community leaders and 1500 Anganwadi Centres (AWCs) from 300 ICDS
projects across 35 States/UTs. Some of the key findings of the study report are :
(i) About two third (64 per cent) of the children received supplementary nutrition. Against
the norm of 25 days a month, on an average they received food for 16 days in a
month.
(ii) Overall 42.5 per cent of sampled AWCs have their own buildings, 17.4 per cent are
in rented buildings, 17.3 per cent are located in primary schools and the 22.9 per cent
are running from A WW/AWH house, panchayat and community buildings.
(iii) Country-wide, a total of about 87 per cent AWCs were found to have drinking water
supply.
(iv) 69 per cent of sampled AWWs having functional baby weighing scale;
(v) About 94 per cent of sampled AWWs reported to have been adequately trained to
conduct pre-school education;
(vi) About 40 per cent of AWWs reported getting some help from Panchayat with about
36 per cent in monitoring and 34 per cent in providing infrastructure. About 70 per
cent of the community leaders felt that the ICDS program was very useful to the
community;
(vii) A verage attendance of number of children 3-6 yrs based on three sudden visits by the
Research Team was found to be 14.
(viii) Intended behavioural changes of varied intensity have been observed in Kerala,
Himachal Pradesh Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Maharashtra, West Bengal and
Jharkhand. In general, the practice of breast feeding within an hour of birth is found
to be more widespread among ICDS beneficiaries;
(ix) ICDS have also positively influenced formal school enrolment and reduction in early
discontinuation among beneficiaries;
(x) At the national level, ICDS programme has impacted the immunization coverage,
especially measles vaccination.
4.28 The Committee takes note of the various findings of the study and suggests that
more initiatives should be taken to improve the programme implementation. The Ministry
should innovate new ways to tackle malnutrition, for example, use of technology to identify

V. INTEGRATED CHILD PROTECTION SCHEME (ICPS)
5.1 The Ministry of Women and Child Development is implementing a Centrally sponsored
scheme “Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS)” with a view to create a safe and secure
environment for comprehensive development of children who are in need of care and protection,
children in conflict with law and other vulnerable children. This scheme is being implemented from
financial year 2009-10 mainly through the State Governments/UT Administrations. The financial
norms have been revised w.e.f. 1 st April, 2014 with enhanced financial norms.
5.2 The programme components include:–
● Support to Statutory Structures such as Child Welfare Committees (CWCs) and Juvenile
Justice Boards (JJBs).
● Institutional Services: Shelter Homes, Children’s Homes, Observation Homes, Special
Homes and Specialized services for children with special needs (disabled & children
affected by HIV/AIDS).
● Dedicated Service delivery structures at Central, State and District levels.
● Family based non-institutional care through: Sponsorship, Foster care, Adoption and
After Care Programme.
● Open shelters for children in need in urban and semi-urban areas.
● Emergency outreach service for children in difficult circumstances through childline.
● Child Tracking System including a website for missing children.
5.3 The Committee was informed that considerable progress has been made under ICPS in
establishing statutory bodies. 636 Child Welfare Committees (240 before introduction of the
Scheme) and 635 Juvenile Justice Boards (211 before introduction of the Scheme) have so far been
established all over the country. To ensure that proper focus is maintained on child protection and
quality of services is up to the mark, the scheme envisages creating a service delivery network,
exclusively for child protection which has been provided with setting up and maintenance of 34
State Child Protection Societies, 32 State Project Support Units, 32 State Adoption Resource
Agencies and 636 District Child Protection Units. Upto 31st December, 2014, under the scheme,
317 Specialized Adoption Agencies (SAAs) and 1501 Homes of various types have been funded. In
the financial year, 2014-15 proposals of 33 States/UTs and Childline India Foundation have been
considered by the inter-Ministerial Project Approval Board (PAB), set up for appraisal and approval
of the financial proposals received under the Scheme. In 2014-15, `329.50 crores have been
sanctioned and released upto 31 st December, 2014 under the Scheme as against the previous year’s
expenditure of `263.38 crores. The budget allocation for the year 2015-16 is `402.23 crores as
against the projected demand of `700 crores. The status of the Scheme with respect to budgetary

5.5 Committee’s attention has been drawn to the various concerns raised regarding the number
and welfare of children who are found on the streets of large cities, either begging or performing
petty jobs. It was given to understand by the Ministry that in order to address this issue, the
Scheme of “ An Integrated Programme for Street Children ” has been merged into the ICPS under
the component of “Open Shelters”. The Open Shelter will provide facilities, with considerably
enhanced financial norms, for temporary shelter, bridge education, entertainment, food, medical
facilities etc. Funds are provided to the State Governments for running these open shelters by
themselves or through NGOs on a similar cost sharing basis.
5.6 Working Children are identified as children in need of care and protection under the Juvenile
Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2000, amended in 2006. Therefore even though the
Ministry of Labour is the nodal Ministry dealing with child labour, MWCD is also implementing a
‘Scheme for Welfare of Working Children in Need of Care and Protection’ as well under which
funds are released to NGOs on a 90:10 sharing basis to provide facilities such as non-formal
education, vocational training, counseling, stipend, nutrition etc. for working children, so as to
facilitate their entry into the mainstream education system. This programme is implemented in urban
areas not covered by the Ministry of Labour under its National Child Labour Project.
5.7 The Scheme for Welfare of Working Children in Need of Care and Protection was
evaluated by National Institute of Public Cooperation and Child Development (NIPCCD) and the
Scheme was found to be achieving desired results of mainstreaming the beneficiary children.
However, subsequent to the evaluation, a Committee was set up in the Ministry to suggest
changes in the Scheme, based on outcome on the evaluation. It was recommended that, as the
Open Shelter component of the Ministry’s newly introduced scheme, ICPS provides similar
services under its Open Shelter component, albeit with better norms and procedures, the projects
under the scheme for Welfare of Working Children be covered under ICPS and this scheme be
phased out.
5.8 Attention of the Committee is being drawn to the increasing incidents of rampant sexual
abuse of children in orphanages/shelter homes involving in-house caretakers. The Ministry, in this
regard, has requested the States/UTs to focus on the implementation of the Juvenile Justice (Care
and Protection of Children) Act, 2000 which is mandatory for establishing a juvenile justice system

17
based on the principle of a child-friendly approach and is in the best interest of children. The Act
focuses on providing for proper care, protection and treatment by catering to their development
needs of the children for their ultimate rehabilitation and prevention of all kinds of abuse. The
Ministry has also urged the States/UTs to strengthen the mechanism for stringent monitoring of
quality of services at the Homes through Child Welfare Committees and inspection committees that
are to be set up by the State Government at State, district and city levels and to make efforts
towards social auditing for the purpose of monitoring and evaluation of Homes to prevent any
abuse or exploitation of children.
5.9 As per Section 34(3) of the JJ Act, which provides for mandatory registration of all
institutions housing children in need of care and protection with the intent of enforcing minimum
standards of care for the services provided for children in these Homes, the Ministry has been
strongly advocating the States/UTs to identify and register all Child Care Institutions under the Act
at the earliest.
5.10 The Ministry has also enacted the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012,
under which the abuse of children by management or staff of any hospital, educational or religious
institution or a jail, remand home, protection home, observation home, or other place of custody
or care and protection is regarded as an aggravated offence with stringent punishments.
5.11 The provisions of registration of Child Care Institutions (CCIs) and their inspections
have been made stringent in the JJ Bill, 2014 that has been presented in the Parliament on
12
th August, 2014. Under the JJ Bill, 2014, the Ministry has made it mandatory for registration of
institutions whether run by State Government or by voluntary or non-Governmental organizations,
which are meant, either wholly or partially, for housing children in need of care and protection of
children in conflict with law are to be mandatorily registered under the Act within six months from
the date of commencement of the Act.
5.12 The inspection committees constituted under Section 55 of the Bill are required to conduct
visits to all facilities housing children in the area allocated, at least once in three months and submit
reports to the State Government. The Juvenile Justice Board (JJB) under Section 9 and the Child
Welfare Committee (CWC) under section 31 are required to mandatorily conduct at least two
inspection visits per month of residential facilities for children in conflict with law and children in
need of care and protection. In case of abuse of child in an institution, the JJB can order the police
for registration of FIR.
5.13 The Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS) provides for hiring of contractual staff at
State and District level. In order to appoint competent and professionally qualified personnel, the
contractual posts are to be advertised through national/local dailies and personnel recruited on the
basis of qualifications, experience, high degree of motivation and commitment to children’s causes.
Individual terms of reference (TOR) are to be drawn up for each post by the State Government.
All recruitments shall be made as per the guidelines of the respective Governments.
5.14 The Committee was assured that while selecting the staff for a girl’s home, every effort
shall be made to appoint female personnel, especially at leadership and decision-making levels as
well as those interacting with the girl children. In order to facilitate the S tate Governments/UTs to
appoint qualified and experienced staff, the Ministry has revised the salaries of all the staff of the

salaries of senior staff-the counselor and Superintendent from `10,000 and `15,000 per month

Inspection of Homes
5.15 The Ministry has been taking initiatives for conducting inspections of various kinds of
Homes in co-ordination with the State Governments. The Ministry constitutes teams including its
own officials and from the State Governments to visit the Homes of different kinds of children
in need of care and protection and children in conflict with law. The objective of these inspections
is to check the standards of care being followed in these homes on one hand and to gain an insight
into the challenges being faced by the management of these Child Care Institutions (CCIs) in
running these Homes.
5.16 In 2014-15, the Ministry conducted inspections in four States namely Odisha, Rajasthan,
West Bengal and Madhya Pradesh. The inspection teams visited one observation home, one Children
home, one open shelter and one Specialized Adoption Agencies in two districts of the above
mentioned State, being managed by the Government as well as Non-Governmental Organizations.
The teams were provided inspection checklists for each of the different kind of Home for

● Inadequate staff at the homes
● Homes not being run as mandated in the JJ Act
● Number of children housed than the sanctioned strength
● Inadequate bathrooms and toilets
● Life skill and vocational training missing
● Local community not involved in activities
5.17 The Committee would like to express its satisfaction over the various steps taken
to deal with the issue of sexual abuse of children. The Committee welcomes the positive
steps taken by the Ministry in coordination with other concerned agencies and the State
Governments/UT Administrations. The need of the hour is the proper implementation of the
various provisions laid down in the Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act,
2000. It is also important that the States/UTs make an effort to implement the Act to
punish the perpetrators and also to prevent further committing of crimes. Moreover, the
Committee feels that public at large needs to be made aware of these legal provisions and
facilities available to the victims so that committing of any such crimes be prevented and
justice be served.
VI. BETI BACHAO BETI PADHAO (BBBP) PROGRAMME
6.1 The Census (2011) showed a significant declining trend in the Child Sex Ratio (CSR), with
an all-time low of 918 in age group of 0-6 years per 1000 boys. The Prime Minister has launched
Beti Bachao, Beti Padhao (BBBP) programme on 22
nd January, 2015 at Panipat, Haryana to address
the issue of declining CSR through a mass campaign across the country and focused intervention
and multi-sectoral action in 100 selected districts low on CSR. The overall goal of the BBBP
Programme is to celebrate Girl Child and enable her to get education. It is a joint initiative of
Ministry of Women and Child Development, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare and Ministry
of Human Resource Development.
6.2 Targets under BBBP Programme:–

19
(a) Improving the nutrition status by reducing number of underweight and anaemic girls
under 5 years of age is one of targets under the scheme. This is being done in
convergence with the existing schemes of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
such as Janani Suraksha Yojana and National Health Mission, as well as the schemes/
programmes of the Ministry such as ICDS, Sabla and IGMSY .
(b) To ensure girls attendance in School following intervention has been envisaged under
BBBP Scheme through Ministry of Human Resource Development:
● Activate School Management Committees (SMCs) to ensure universal enrolment of
girls;
● Campaign to re-enroll drop-out girls in secondary schools
● Girl Child friendly standards in schools;
● Strict implementation of Rights to Education (RTE);
● Construction of Functioned Toilets for girls.
(c) To enable environment of protection and survival of girl child following intervention
has been envisaged under the BBBP Scheme by the Ministry of WCD and Ministry of
Health and Family Welfare
(i) Ministry of Women and Child Development
● Nation-wide Media Campaign aimed to ensure that girls are born, nurtured and
educated without discrimination to become empowered citizens of this country
with equal rights.
● Promote registration of pregnancies in first trimester in Anganwadi Centres
(AWCs);
● Implement a sustained Social Mobilization and Communication Campaign to

6.3 The Committee observes that the steadily declining child sex ratio in India has
reached emergency proportions and urgent action must be taken to alleviate this crisis. The
Committee further observes that this decline has taken place despite the best efforts by the
Ministry in checking this trend. It should be noted that girl child is the future of every
nation and India is no exception. In a society, both girls and boys, play equally important
roles. To eliminate girl child from the society is a step backward, away from the civilized
society. So, for the society and the nation as a whole to grow and progress, the girl child
must be saved, cared, nurtured and loved. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Ministry should make all out efforts to check this declining CSR in a mission mode and
also to put more aggressiveness, energy and resources to reverse this trend.
VII. RAJIV GANDHI SCHEME FOR EMPOWERMENT OF ADOLESCENT GIRLS
(RGSEAG)-SABLA
7.1 Rajiv Gandhi Scheme for empowerment of adolescent girls-SABLA was introduced on a
pilot basis in August 2010 and is operational in 205 selected districts across the country. SABLA
aims at all round development of adolescent girls of 11-18 years (with a focus on all out-of school
adolescent girls) by making them ‘self-reliant’ by improving their health and nutrition status,
promoting awareness about health, hygiene, nutrition, Adolescent Reproductive and Sexual Health
(ARSH), family and child care and facilitating access to learning about public services through
various interventions such as guidance and counseling as well as V ocational Training. It also aims
towards mainstreaming ‘out of school adolescent girls into formal/non-formal education. The
scheme has two major components Nutrition and non Nutrition Component. SABLA is an
intervention which addresses the health needs of Adolescent Girls(AGs) and will not only lead to
a healthier and more productive women force but will also help to break the intergenerational cycle
of malnutrition.
7.2 The Ministry submitted that nutrition is being given in the form of Take Home Ration or
Hot Cooked Meal for 11-14 years out of school girls and 14-18 years to all Adolescent Girls (out
of school and in school girls). Each adolescent girl is given 600 calories and 18-20 grams of
protein and micronutrients (which is approx. 1/3 of recommended dietary allowances) per day for
300 days in a year. The out of school adolescent girls (11-14 years) attending AWCs and all girls
(14-18 years) are provided Supplementary nutrition in the form of Take Home Ration/Hot Cooked
Meal. The nutrition provided is as per the norms for P&L mothers.
7.3 While the nutrition component aims at improving the health and nutrition status of the
adolescent girls the non-nutrition component addresses the developmental needs. In the Non
Nutrition Component, out of school adolescent girls of 11-18 years are being provided IFA
supplementation, health check-up and referral services, nutrition a nd health ed ucation , ARSH
counseling/guidance on accessing public services and vocational training (only 16-18 year old
adolescent girls.).
7.4 The Scheme targets to provide nutrition to 1 crore adolescent girls. The scheme is proposed
to be continued in 2015-16 with revised nutrition (@ `.7 per beneficiary per day for 300 days in
a year against the present rate of `.5/beneficiary/day and non-nutrition norms ( `7 lakh per project
per annum against the present rate of `3.8 lakh/project/annum).

VIII.  INDIRA GANDHI MATRITVA SAHYOG YOJANA (IGMSY)
8.1 Indira Gandhi Matritva Sahyog Yojna (IGMSY) is a conditional Cash Transfer Scheme for
Pregnant and Lactating (P&L) women who are 19 years of age or above. It was introduced in
October 2010 in 53 pilot districts to contribute to better enabling environment by providing
maternity benefit @ `4000 per beneficiary for first two live births. Objective of the scheme is to
improve the health and nutrition status and partly compensate for wage loss of the P&L women.
Maternity benefit was revised to `6000.00 w.e.f. 05
th July, 2013 as per the provisions of the
National Food Security Act, 2013.
8.2 The Scheme provides benefit to all pregnant and lactating women except for all
Government/PSUs (Central and State) employees, as they are entitled for paid maternity leave.
From 259 beneficiaries in 2010-11 the scheme covered 5.70 lakhs beneficiaries in 2013-14,
irrespective of the fact that they belonged to the Below Poverty Line (BPL) or Above Poverty Line
(APL). The beneficiaries are paid `6000 in two equal installments per P&L women on fulfilling
specific conditions related to maternal and child health to partly compensate for wage loss to
mothers/women during pregnancy and period of lactation. The cash incentives through provision
of Conditional Cash Transfer (CCT) would, not only, contribute to better enabling environment but
also encourage and promote health and nutrition. The Scheme is now covered under Direct Benefit
Transfer (DBT) programme and under which 16 districts have been included under Phase-I and
Phase-II of the implementation.
8.3 The Ministry pointed out that the proposal for continuation and expansion of IGMSY
has been approved by the Expenditure Finance Committee (EFC) in its meeting held on
9

IX. CENTRAL ADOPTION RESOURCE AGENCY (CARA)
9.1 Central Adoption Resource Agency (CARA) is an autonomous body under the Ministry of
Women and Child Development, Government of India. It functions as the nodal body for adoption
of Indian children and is mandated to monitor and regulate in-country and inter-country adoptions.
CARA is designated as the Central Authority to deal with inter-country adoptions in accordance
with the provisions of the Hague Convention on Inter-country Adoption, 1993, ratified by
Government of India in 2003.
9.2 Functions of CARA:
● To function as a nodal body in the country on matters related to adoption;
● To evolve a structure for non-institutional child care services in the country and to
standardize, streamline and implement such services;
● To build an environment that provides an opportunity for every adoptable child in the
country to find a suitable family.

24
● To frame rules and guidelines for adoption of Indian children and ensure their proper
implementation;
● To regulate and monitor adoptions and maintain a database on adoptions done in the
country;
● To prepare a centralized database of all children and PAP(s) with the help of its
associated agencies for the purpose of establishing central and state level information
pool on orphan, abandoned and surrendered children and waiting parents;
● To carry out research and documentation on adoption in order to continuously improve
the adoption system;
● To arrange capacity building programmes for adoption agencies, and other stakeholders
engaged in child welfare activities;
● To carry out advocacy, awareness and IEC activities for promoting non institutional
child care services either by itself or through its associated bodies.
● To coordinate with all State Government, State Adoption Resource Agencies (SARAs)
and support them in adoption related matters;
● To monitor the status of children placed adoption and to maintain information and
records of all such children for the purpose of follow up and root-search.
● To liaison with the other Central Authorities and foreign Missions to ensure post-
adoption follow-up and care for the adopted children.

X. RASHTRIYA MAHILA KOSH (RMK)
10.1 The Rashtriya Mahila Kosh (RMK), an Apex micro-finance organization under the Ministry
of Women and Child Development, exclusively for women was set up in 1993 for the purpose of
providing micro-loans to poor women through Government and Non-government organizations,
women federations and cooperative banks.  RMK extends loans through a client friendly, without
collateral and hassle-free mechanism for livelihoods, micro-enterprises, housing and family needs in
both rural and urban areas. RMK has taken a number of promotional measures to popularize the
concept of micro financing, thrift and credit, formation and stabilization of Self Help Groups
(SHGs) and also enterprise development for poor women.
10.2 RMK works as a single-window organization. Apart from giving micro-credit, it also builds
the capacities of Self Help Groups/women members and partner organizations through trainings in
financial management, enterprise development, skills and modern management practices, as well as
exposure visits and assistance in marketing. In addition, the partner organizations that take loans
from RMK are instructed to impart literacy, legal education, health awareness etc. to the women
beneficiaries to bring about their holistic empowerment. RMK views micro-finance as development
finance. RMKs micro finance programs for the socio-economic upliftment of poor women are
dispensed through NGOs/SHGs. These NGOs may be voluntary organizations, Government
autonomous bodies; Co-operative societies etc. to work as Financial Intermediary Organization
(IMOs).
10.3 The RMK has extended its IMOs network across the Nicobar Island and the border areas
of Jammu and Kashmir. As on 31.12.2014, RMK has sanctioned cumulative loans of `360.24 crore
benefitting 7,35,239 women. Out of this sum of 302.28 crore was disbursed. Details of loans

on improvement in the living condition of poor women beneficiaries. This study was performed in
9 States (Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Delhi, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha, Rajasthan, Tamil
Nadu and West Bengal. The scope of this study included in depth interaction with the 15
Intermediary Organizations (IMOs) and to assess socio-economic impact on 1500 beneficiaries
from 500 women SHGs. The findings of the study are as follows:
1. Members of the groups were mostly (57 per cent) women from BPL families.
2. RMK loan has covered vigorously young work force (72 per cent of the beneficiaries)
3. RMK micro financing in the rural areas had a positive impact on backward classes of
the society as 46 per cent of OBC, 22 per cent of scheduled caste and 11 per cent
of scheduled tribe population had been covered under RMK loan.
4. Majority of the beneficiaries (85 per cent) came to know about SHGs through NGO/
IMOs followed by funds and other sources.
5. The survey indicated active involvement of beneficiaries in different kinds of self-
employment generating micro enterprise.
6. The average savings per member per annum before joining the SHG was `1961 which
was increased to `2993 after becoming the members of the SHGs.
7. Majority of the beneficiaries (95 per cent) had improved their usage of medical facility
after seeking RMK loan.
8. There was noticeable change in the consumption pattern and a better household
nutrition through SHG activities.
10.6   The Committee is happy to note the positive outcomes of the scheme of RMK
which has led to economic empowerment of poor women in the identified States as
highlighted in the impact assessment studies. Not just this, economic empowerment of these
women also resulted in increasing their self-confidence and awareness and has given them
respect and a say in decision making leading to their social empowerment. The Committee
believes that in order to sustain and increase the reach of the scheme to the targeted
women, sustained efforts need to be made by the Ministry to utilize the allocated funds and
closely monitor the progress of the Scheme.

XI. HOSTELS FOR WORKING WOMEN
11.1    Under the Scheme of Working Women Hostel, financial assistance as provided for
construction/running of Hostel in rented premises for those working women who may be single,
widowed, divorced, separated, married but whose husband or immediate family does not reside in
the same area and for those women  who are under training for job.  Provision of day care centre

XIV. NATIONAL MISSION FOR THE EMPOWERMENT OF WOMEN (NMEW)
14.1 The Committee observes that National Mission for the Empowerment of W omen (NMEW)
under Ministry of Women and Child Development was initiated during the terminal year of the
Eleventh plan to bring about inter-sectoral convergence with a gender focus. NMEW aims to
achieve holistic empowerment of women through convergence of schemes/programmes of different
Ministries/Department of Government of India as well as State Governments.
14.2 The Scheme entailed setting up National Resource Centre for Women (NRCW), State
Resource Centre for Women (SRCW) in States/UTs and community based resource centres
(known as Poorna Shakti Kendra) at select district and sub-district/community level for
facilitating inter-sectoral convergence is being facilitated in coordination with partner Ministries
at the central level.
14.3 NMEW is implementing thematic projects in collaboration with various civil society
organizations/institutes working in the area of women’s empowerment. The projects have been
selected for their innovativeness covering diverse themes critical for empowerment of women, and
across different regions.
14.4   NMEW is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) from Eleventh Five Year Plan and proposed
for continuation in the Twelfth Plan. However, modifications have been proposed in thrust areas

29
and structures in the current proposal which envisages restructuring of the scheme for
implementation in the Twelfth Plan with the following objectives:
(i) To strengthen efforts towards achieving empowerment of women in India. This
will be done through the NRCW and SRCWs which will support the Ministry of
WCD at the centre and Department of WCD/Social W elfare in the States/UTs
respectively.
(ii) To facilitate convergence and coordination for women related Schemes and
Programmes at national, state and sub-state level. Convergence centres and outreach
services for women will be provided in selected gender critical districts to enable
greater awareness and utilization of schemes/programmes meant for women.
(iii) Enhance community’s participation through community platforms/services under
Village Convergence and Facilitation Service (VCFS) in 100 gender critical districts to
address social evils like dowry, domestic violence, declining Child Sex Ratio, violence
against Women etc.
(iv) Function as a training and capacity building resource centre both at Centre and State
levels to enhance understanding and sensitivity of various stakeholders on gender
related issues.
(v) Develop a web based resource portal or women.
14.5 The Committee notes that the budgetary allocation for NMEW was `90 crore for the year
2014-15 which was reduced to `8 crore. The Ministry submitted that the scheme was in the
process of appraisal by the EFC and the implementation of certain components of the scheme was
under review. The scheme has since been approved with costs sharing with States/UTs. The
Scheme as has been approved shall be implemented from the financial year 2015-16. Pending
completion of the process of appraisal and approval, the release of grant to States/UTs could not
be processed.
14.6 The Committee is of the considered view that the objective of the ‘National Mission
for Empowerment of Women’ is of vital importance as it aims at social, economic and
educational empowerment of women. The Committee feels that the scheme has not taken
off properly even though five years had passed since the Scheme had been launched. The
Committee feels that it is high time that the objectives of the Mission are achieved through
its proper implementation.  The Committee hopes that all pending procedures for appraisal
and approval are completed without any delay and that the Scheme starts to function
efficiently.
XV.  NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR WOMEN (NCW)
15.1   National Commission for Women (NCW) was constituted on 31 st January, 1992 as a
statutory body at the National level, to safeguard and promote the rights and interests of women.
The Commission investigates and examines the legal safeguards provided to women under the
Constitution and other laws and recommends to Government, the measures for their effective
implementation. The Commission is also authorized to review the existing provisions of the
Constitution and other laws affecting women and recommend amendments to meet any lacunae,

XVII. GENDER BUDGETING
17.1 Gender Budgeting is a powerful tool for addressing gender based disparities and achieving
women empowerment through mainstreaming gender corners across sector. Gender budgeting
enables in maintaining a gender perspective at all stages, including formulation of policies and
schemes, allocation of policies and schemes, allocation of resources, implementation, monitoring
and review. It leads to translation of gender commitments into budgetary commitments.
17.2 A Plan Scheme for Gender Budgeting was launched in the year 2008 during the Eleventh
Plan period, for conducting, training/workshops, capacity building, research surveys etc. Under the
Scheme, inter alia , the Ministry undertakes many programmes as well as provides financial support
for the purpose. An outlay of `1.30 crore (at RE stage) was allocated for the Scheme in the year
2014-15, for conducting various training programmes and workshops on Gender Budgeting. Out of
which, an amount of `1.07 crore have been incurred till January, 2015. An amount `2.00 crore

33
(BE) has been allocated for the year 2015-16. The Committee notes that so far 57 Ministries/
Departments have set up Gender Budgeting Cells. A total of 18 States and 3 UTs have undertaken
various Gender Budgeting Initiatives.
17.3 The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Women and Child Development
being the nodal agency for gender budgeting should focus upon the proper allocation to and
full utilization of the Gender Budgeting Scheme. There has been a considerable progress
made in this area which have concerns across the Ministries both at the Central and State
level from the perspective of women specific schemes. The focus should be aimed at
strengthening and empowering the Gender Budgeting Cells to enable them to undertake
their envisaged role effectively.
17.4 Like Gender Budgeting, Child Budgeting can be considered another major initiative
in sensitizing and institutionalizing child-related concerns. For this purpose, the Committee
notes that the Ministry will have to build capacities to analyse the Central and State
budgets and their impact on the betterment children.
XVIII. CONCLUSION
18.1 The Ministry of Women and Child Development was set up as a nodal agency with
the prime aim to empower and promote holistic development and welfare of women and
children who are considered the vulnerable sections of society. The Ministry has formulated
many women and child centred legislations, plans, policies and programmes to ensure
women’s empowerment as well as gender equality to the extent possible and to ensure
children’s holistic development and growth. The Committee is aware that the Ministry has
to cater to more than 70 per cent of the total population and that too the most vulnerable
ones. It, therefore, has indeed a massive responsibility. The Committee finds the
performance of the Ministry satisfactory but still a lot more needs to be done, particularly
for arresting the rising crimes against women and children. The Committee strongly feels
that the Ministry should ensure safety and security to women including at the workplace,
by ending all forms of discrimination, exploitation, harassment and violence against women
by strictly implementing the relevant laws promulgated for the purpose. Further, the
Ministry should strive towards ensuring zero tolerance to all kinds of exploitation of
children including child labour, sexual abuse and violence, by providing legislative and
institutional support. The Committee is of the view that the Ministry would find it very
difficult to fulfill the objectives of empowerment of women in all walks of life due to
massive cut in funds this year. The Committee also feels that it should have better
coordination with the State Governments and various agencies, NGOs for implementing
women/children centric schemes for more better results.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERV ATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE — AT A GLANCE
II BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
The Committee is dismayed to note that there has been a substantial decrease in
budgetary allocation in child welfare schemes. The same is the case with the schemes
related to women also. Though the Finance Minister has announced in this year’s budgetary
speech (Para 55) that extra resources of around `1500 crores would be provided as
depending on additional resources. However, the Ministry seems to have been caught
unawares about such a massive budget cut. Devolution of funds to the States as per
recommendation of the Fourteenth Finance Commission is yet to concretize. Even if it
comes, the experience with States contributing their share had not been very encouraging.
So, with this budget cut, there is a question mark as to how and when these States would
contribute remaining part. Thus, the Ministry has been left in lurch affecting the very
implementation of the existing Schemes. The Committee, however, recommends that all out
efforts be made to see that the State Governments contribute their share as soon as
possible so that the projected targets can be achieved efficiently and in a timely manner.
The Committee also recommends that the Ministry of Finance should make `1500 crores as
promised by Minister of Finance before Parliament at the earliest lest the schemes of the
Department should suffer. (Para 2.3)
The Committee observes that in almost all the major schemes, except only one
scheme namely, National Commission for Women, BE allocation has been drastically brought
down at the RE stage. Further, it is unfortunate to note that in the major schemes, the
funds allocated have not been utilized to the fullest extent. Also in the scheme of National
Nutrition Mission, the utilization of funds is nil and for the scheme of One Stop Crisis
Centre, no fund had been allocated in the RE stage in the year 2014-15. The Committee
would like to point out that in major schemes like ICDS and SABLA, the funds allocated
in BE 2015-16 has been cut to great extent that the achieving the physical targets of these
schemes might have been affected.  This needs to be checked and the Committee desires
that a status note on this be furnished to the Committee for its consideration.  (Para 2.5)
The Committee observes from the reason given by the Ministry for non-utilization
that these social sector schemes were included in the Ministry’s budget in anticipation that
these would be approved for the implementation. But for 2 schemes out of 8, none could
be approved. Therefore, the budgetary allocation has not been utilized. It also appears to
be the main reason for reduction in allocations at RE stage during these years. The
Committee takes a serious view of such an approach on the part of the Ministry in this
regard and recommends that it should have made serious attempt to get all the approvals
for the implementation of the Schemes for better utilization of funds. (Para 2.7)
The Committee finds that the performance of the Scheme like SABLA has been
satisfactory, however for the IGMSY Scheme, the physical targets remained under-achieved
in 2013-14 and 2014-15. Schemes related for girl child, adolescent girls and women are of
vital importance, so any problems faced in the achievement of targets need to be identified
and addressed for the efficacious implementation of the schemes. (Para 2.9)
The Committee notes the concerted efforts made by the Ministry to liquidate the
pending UCs and the progress made so far. However, it would like to point out that in spite

of their efforts, there is still a good number of UCs that are pending. Consistent efforts on
the part of the Ministry are required for liquidation of the remaining UCs. Constraints
faced in the procedural formalities and accounting system need to be identified and

efficient implementation of these Schemes. There is a need for efforts to provide flexibility

resources and the need for funding schemes with realistic cost norms. Policy formulation,
strengthening programmes execution, enforcement of laws, plan implementation, capacity-

(Para 15.7)
During the deliberations of the committee, the issue of non-existence of any
schemes/activities for protection and welfare of women under Nirbhaya Fund was raised. The
Committee understands that no substantial schemes/programmes have been finalized
although allocations of funds were available for the purpose for the last 2 to 3 years.  The
Committee would like to point out that the Nirbhaya Fund had a total of 3000 crore as 1000
crore each was allocated to it in 2014-15 and 2015-16 on top of `1000 crore intial corpus.
The Fund has been lying un-utilized for last three years. No clear strategy has come up to
ensure proper utilization of the fund allocated. On a specific query regarding this issue, the
Ministry replied that the Ministry of Surface Transport had come up with the proposal of
about `1400 crores, which has been already sanctioned. Also, the Ministry of Home Affairs
has also come up with a comprehensive scheme for about `321 crore. The Committee
observes that the Ministry has not come up with any concrete action plan to utilize this
Fund. Women safety is a major priority and to deal with and prevent the rising crimes
against women, it is high time that the Ministry comes up with steps to ensure women
safety. The Committee also desires that a status note on the use of this Fund may be
submitted to the Committee at the earliest for its perusal. (Para 15.9)
XVI. RESEARCH, PUBLICATION AND MONIORING, INFORMATION AND MASS
The Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need for having a re-look of
different activities to be undertaken for better implementation as well as expanding reach
of different schemes. A comprehensive advocacy and awareness generation policy and plan
of action has to be developed and implemented that will ensure public awareness about the
existing policies and programmes for women and children at all levels. Hence, the
Committee recommends that all out efforts be made to create public awareness about the
schemes/programmes of the Ministry. (Para 16.2)

41
XVII. GENDER BUDGETING
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Women and Child Development
being the nodal agency for gender budgeting should focus upon the proper allocation to and
full utilization of the Gender Budgeting Scheme. There has been a considerable progress
made in this area which have concerns across the Ministries both at the Central and State
level from the perspective of women specific schemes. The focus should be aimed at
strengthening and empowering the Gender Budgeting Cells to enable them to undertake
their envisaged role effectively. (Para 17.3)
Like Gender Budgeting, Child Budgeting can be considered another major initiative
in sensitizing and institutionalizing child-related concerns. For this purpose, the Committee
notes that the Ministry will have to build capacities to analyse the Central and State
budgets and their impact on the betterment children. (Para 17.4)
XVIII. CONCLUSION
The Ministry of Women and Child Development was set up as a nodal agency with
the prime aim to empower and promote holistic development and welfare of women and
children who are considered the vulnerable sections of society. The Ministry has formulated
many women and child centred legislations, plans, policies and programmes to ensure
women’s empowerment as well as gender equality to the extent possible and to ensure
children’s holistic development and growth. The Committee is aware that the Ministry has
to cater to more than 70 per cent of the total population and that too the most vulnerable
ones. It, therefore, has indeed a massive responsibility. The Committee finds the
performance of the Ministry satisfactory but still a lot more needs to be done, particularly
for arresting the rising crimes against women and children. The Committee strongly feels
that the Ministry should ensure safety and security to women including at the workplace,
by ending all forms of discrimination, exploitation, harassment and violence against women
by strictly implementing the relevant laws promulgated for the purpose. Further, the
Ministry should strive towards ensuring zero tolerance to all kinds of exploitation of
children including child labour, sexual abuse and violence, by providing legislative and
institutional support. The Committee is of the view that the Ministry would find it very
difficult to fulfill the objectives of empowerment of women in all walks of life due to
massive cut in funds this year. The Committee also feels that it should have better
coordination with the State Governments and various agencies, NGOs for implementing
women/children centric schemes for more better results. (Para 18.1)

REPORT
1. INTRODUCTION
Department of Sports is a Department under the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports.
Sports and Games have always been perceived as an integral component in the all-round
development of personality. Apart from being a means of entertainment and physical fitness, sports
have always played a greater role in generating spirit of healthy competition and bonding among
us. Today, sports emerge as an important component of socio-economic development of the
country and the Government plays a crucial role in promoting sports. The Government and
governmental organizations are responsible in making sports policies, allocating grants for
developing infrastructure, nurturing talents and designing specialized programmes for overall
development of sports.
2. Today, many types of sports are played across the country. Things apart, regional games
have also become a way of life. India first participated at the Summer Olympic Games in 1920,
and, since then, has participated in every Summer Olympic Games. India’s first achievement in
Gold Medal in Olympics dates back to the 1928 Summer Olympic Games, winning Men’s Field
Hockey. Abhinav Bindra became the first Indian to win an individual Gold Medal at the Olympic
Games.
3. India’s performance is disheartening among nations for having won very few Olympic
Medals, despite a population of over 1.2 billion. Several explanations, among others, have been
attributed for abysmal performance which inter alia includes poverty, mal-nutrition, neglected
infrastructure, lack of sponsorship, institutional disor ganization, etc. As regards Commonwealth
Games, India has competed in fourteen out of the eighteen previous Commonwealth Games. Since
the inception in 1934, India hosted the games once in 2010. India is fourth most successful
country with a total of 436 Medals including 156 Gold Medals.
4. The year 1982 is significant in the history of sports in India as India organized the IX Asian
Games in Delhi . Prior to that not much emphasis had been given towards sports in public policies.
National Sports Policy, 1984 was the first move towards developing an organized and systematic
framework for the development and promotion of sports in the country, and the precursor of the
present National Sports Policy, 2001. The twin planks of the National Sports Policy 2001 are
“Broad-basing of Sports” and “Achieving Excellence in Sports” at the national and international
levels. The salient features of the Policy are as:–
➢ Broad-basing of sports and achievement of excellence;
➢ Upgradation and development of infrastructure;
➢ Support to National Sports Federations and other sports bodies;
➢ Strengthening of scientific and coaching support to sports;
➢ Special incentives to promote sports;
➢ Enhanced participation of women, scheduled tribes and rural youth;
➢ Involvement of corporate sector in sports promotion; and
➢ Promote sports mindedness among the public at large.
5. With increased exposure to global sporting events, there is a growing market today for new
sports. The phenomenal rise in the youth population has made India youngest nation with a
demographic dividend appearing to be a reality. Undoubtedly, young Indians have found a whole

2
new set of sporting heroes. Adding to this, we find a slew of recent wins by Indian sporting icons
which have inspired youngsters to pursue their passion for sports. Based on these developments,
some evident and some latent, it is to be believed that the Indian sports is transcending through
significant changes.
6. The role of the government in the development of sports may be gauzed as threefold –
➢ The Government must allocate land and resources to develop sports facilities.
➢ The Government must create an environment that will allow the grassroot programmes
that are sprouting across the nation to flourish.
➢ All schools should support the initiatives taken by the Government and allocate sufficient
time and resources to physical fitness and sports activities.
Further the Department of Sports, inter alia deals with matters relating to broad-basing of
Sports, anti-doping, uses of sports stadia, etc.
7. The Secretary in his presentation before the Committee on the 17
th April, 2015 gave an
overview of the functioning and status of different schemes/programmes being executed by the
Department. He described that sports is a state subject and it is primarily the responsibility of the
State Governments to create adequate sports infrastructure within the States. Further, the Central
Government complements and supplements efforts of States in this regard. Nevertheless, the
Department of Sports, in the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports, has two primary objectives. One
is broad-basing of sports, that is, of making sports available to all. So, in this context, there are
two major schemes running in the Department. First, which was earlier called as the Panchayat
Yuva Krida and Khel Abhiyan (PYKKA), has now been restructured into the Rajiv Gandhi Khel
Abhiyan (RGKA). Another one is the Urban Sports Infrastructure Scheme, which is for
development of sports infrastructure in the urban centres in the country. The issue regarding the
broad-basing of sports, strictly speaking is not with the Department, however, the efforts are to
encourage sports through the school system. Somehow, it is being transformed as a regular part
of the school curriculum because that is where the real identification, the development of sports
has to automatically come from. The other major objective of the department is in ‘achieving
excellence in sports’. And, in this context, there are two major areas. One is the National Sports
Federation (NSF), which has the responsibility of developing that particular game and also of
selecting the team at the national level, training, nominating the teams for participation in events
and tournaments abroad, and so on. NSFs are autonomous organizations and the Government has
no involvement in their day-to-day working. Second, of course, is the Sports Authority of India
(SAI). The Sports Authority of India has different schemes for identification and nurturing of talent
from the sub-junior level to the elite level. It is also responsible for the training of national teams.
8. The Committee was also apprised of some of the recent initiatives that have been
undertaken. The most important is that of setting of the Manipur Sports University in Manipur. This
was announced in the last year’s Union Budget. The Department is taking steps to get it
established. The site has been identified. The land is likely to be available soon. Second major
initiative, again announced in the last year’s Union Budget, was the National Sports Talent Search
Scheme (NSTSS), which basically deals with identification of sporting talent in the country in the
age group of 8-12 years. The scheme has been developed and notified and the initial selections
should be taking place in September-October this year. The third initiative is the setting up of
national academies in some of our major prominent sports, largely under the aegis of SAI in
collaboration with the National Sports Federations. The fourth is the development of sports
infrastructure in Jammu and Kashmir. This special initiative was announced by the Union Finance
Minister in the last year’s Budget. This basically involves remodeling and renewal of the two major
stadia in Srinagar and Jammu and also development of some sports facilities in district

3
headquarters. Moreover, the Department has two major initiatives which have been going on for
some time now, that is, the setting up of Indian Institute of Sports Science and Medicine and the
National Institute of Sports Coaching. These two projects are still at the formulation stage and will
take some more time for getting established.
9. The Committee was also informed that concerning the performance of individual nations in
medals tally at the Olympic Games, name of Cuba may be cited as an example. Considering that
Cuba’s population is only around 11 million (around half the size of New York metro area), Cuba
is the most successful Olympic team by total medals won. Cuba first participated at the Olympic
Games in 190 0, and had sent athletes to compete in 19 of 27 Summer Olympic Games overall.
Cuban athletes have won a total of 208 medals at the Summer Olympics. In modern Cuban society,
sports and physical education begin from childhood. Children are taught at a later age to play
games that resemble physical exercise. These ideas are the basis for the modern sports
programmes in Cuba, and clearly these are working.

SPORTS AUTHORITY OF  INDIA (SAI)
13. The Sports Authority of India (SAI) is the field arm of the Department and was set up in
1984 as a registered Society. SAI is engaged in spotting and nurturing talent at all levels by
providing the requisite infrastructure and equipment, coaching facilities, scientific back up,
nutritious diet, competition and exposure. It is also entrusted with the responsibility of maintaining

ASSISTANCE TO NATIONAL SPORTS FEDERATIONS
22. The Committee came to know that SAI through its Training of Elite Athletes and
Management Support (TEAMS) Division, provides support to National Sports Federations (NSFs)
by way of coordinating their Long Term Development Plans (LTDPs), and providing logistic and
training support. In this role, a number of activities are being carried out by SAI out of funds
provided to them by the Ministry.
23. The Department recognizes only one federation of each sport discipline at the national level.
The recognized National Sports Federation (NSF), in turn, is responsible for the promotion and
development of the sport. The NSF has to discharge the responsibilities in accordance with the
principles laid down in the Olympic Charter or in the Charter of Indian Olympic Association (IOA),
or the relevant International Federation. The Government only supplements the efforts of National
Sports Federation (NSFs) by providing financial assistance for participation in international events
abroad, conducting national/international tournaments and training/coaching of national teams under
Indian and Foreign Coaches/Experts, etc., under the Scheme of ‘Assistance to national Sports
Federations’. In all these matters, Sports Authority of India (SAI) closely coordinates with NSFs.
24. The Department regularly consults NSFs in major decision making, e.g., the NSFs were
consulted while formulating criteria for Sports Awards, revision of Schemes of the Department,
etc. The Department also either directly or through Sports Authority of India (SAI) consults the
NSFs while implementing its various schemes. The Ministry has evolved an evaluation/performance
monitoring mechanism of the NSFs. Government has also issued instructions to NSFs to
mandatorily declare information on their website pertaining to their audited accounts, balance sheet,
selection criteria for athletes, etc. by 1.4.2015.
25. The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that there is a distinct lack of proper
coordination and control mechanism among the NSFs on the one hand between the Ministry/
SAI and the NSFs on the other hand. The NSFs in the name of their autonomy, the
Committee feels, that they are not accountable to anybody even though they receive
Government funds for their activities. The NSFs, the Committee, feels have a definite role
to play in promoting different sports disciplines in the country. But their working leaves

8
much to be desired. These bodies, unfortunately, devote much of their time and resources
in the non-sporting activities. Most of them have not been able to live upto the
expectations. No doubt, some of them done or doing very good work in the promotion of
sports in the country. The Committee has been expressing its concern over this issue from
time to time and calls upon the Ministry and the representatives of the NSFs to find out
collectively a most efficient and workable solution that can bring our sports sector out of
the present situations. We may perhaps try to learn/adopt the best practices in this respect
from the other countries such as China, Korea, Taiwan, etc.
26. As regards non-compliance of the guidelines, by the NSFs, the Committee was apprised that
the Archery Association of India has been de-recognised since it refused to accept the Government
guidelines; the recognition of Indian Amateur Boxing Federation was suspended and subsequently
the same was not renewed. Recognition to Korfball Football Federation of India has not been
accorded recognition since 2012 for not accepting Government Guidelines. Gymnastics Federation
of India and Athletics Federation of India were asked to hold fresh elections which they have
complied with.
27. The Committee finds it very disheartening on the issue of non-compliance of the
guidelines of the Department by the NSFs and recommends to evolve a suitable mechanism
in this regard so that the preparation as well as participation of the sportspersons in
important national and international events is not affected adversely.

st April, 2014. In the Budget Estimate 2015-16,
